W06000003.research: ACTIVE, established from Conwy's own live licensing page: 'Under our Additional Licensing Scheme there is a different criteria. Additional Licensing only applies to buildings within certain areas of Conwy County. These areas are: Pensarn (Marine Road and South Parade only); Colwyn Bay (within the electoral divisions of Glyn and Rhiw wards only); Llandudno and Craig y Don (within the electoral divisions of Gogarth Mostyn, Tudno and Craig y Don wards only). An HMO in the areas named above must have a licence if: there are three or more tenants living in the building OR they form more than one household, with shared facilities or without shared facilities (typically self-contained flats); the building does not meet the 1991 Building Regulations; Less than two thirds of the self-contained flats are owner occupied.' It separately states the mandatory test, so the two regimes are clearly distinguished. FEE-SCHEDULE TEST, decisive and the reason this is recorded active rather than expired: the page carries a live schedule headed 'Fees are valid from 1 April 2026' with a SEPARATE additional-licensing tier: 'Mandatory licensing: up to 4 lets £819, additional lets over 4 (per let) £145. Additional licensing: up to 4 lets £1,398, additional lets over 4 (per let) £286', with instalment options and worked examples to seven lets (£2,256). A council does not publish a distinct, higher, current-financial-year cost-recovery fee for a designation that has lapsed. DATES NOT PUBLISHED: Conwy publishes no designation notice for the current areas, so start and end are null rather than guessed. The live site was searched for 'designation', 'public notice', 'Pensarn' and 'Craig y Don licensing' and no instrument was found. This is an honest gap and the public note tells landlords to confirm the boundary with the council. SELECTIVE LICENSING: ruled out on a CONTROL-VALIDATED search, which matters because most Conwy tooling is broken. Conwy's site search passes BOTH controls: the positive control 'council tax' returns real relevant results, and the negative control 'zzqqxxvv' returns 'Your search did not match any content.' Against that validated engine, 'selective licensing' ALSO returns 'Your search did not match any content', so that nil result is meaningful. 'multiple occupation', 'HMO' and 'additional licensing' all correctly surface the HMO licensing page, confirming the index covers it. THE EXPIRED PREDECESSOR: Conwy's archived public notice reads 'Notice is hereby given that Conwy County Borough Council has on the 29th day of October 2019 designated an additional licensing scheme in respect of Houses in Multiple Occupation for the electoral ward of Abergele Pensarn... The Scheme will be effective from 1st January 2020 and unless revoked beforehand or extended will cease to have effect on 31st December 2024', citing the Wales 2006 Regulations and s.58(1)(b) and (7). That page now returns 'This page is no longer available'. It is not recorded as a separate scheme object because it is superseded by the current street-based designation covering the same locality. WARDS DELIBERATELY NULL. Checked against the current ONS register: 'Abergele Pensarn' NO LONGER EXISTS (now 'Pen-sarn Pentre Mawr' and 'Gele and Llanddulas'). For the live scheme, Glyn, Rhiw, Gogarth Mostyn and Tudno ARE current Conwy wards, but 'Craig y Don' as the council spells it is not: ONS carries 'Craig-y-don', hyphenated, so an exact-match lookup fails on punctuation alone. More importantly the Pensarn limb is defined by STREETS and the Colwyn Bay and Llandudno limbs are expressly sub-ward ('only'), so a ward list must not be synthesised. Coverage 'areas' with wards null routes these to a boundary check rather than a confident wrong answer in either direction. TRAPS EXCLUDED: Rent Smart Wales, the ONLY licensing regime Conwy's landlord pages mention; 'Additional grant funding of up to £25,000' under Leasing Scheme Wales, a grant not a licence; 'an additional charge of £50' for late applications; 'The Licensing and Management of Houses in Multiple Occupation (Additional Provisions) (Wales) Regulations 2007', the s.257 management instrument; the Llandudno Holiday Accommodation Zone and LDP Policy HOU/10, which are planning; and two apparent 'hmo' hits in the raw HTML that turned out to be fragments inside base64-encoded WebResource.axd blobs. LIMITATIONS: Conwy's sitemap.xml is a 3.4KB stub and useless; its content is JavaScript-rendered so raw curl returns navigation only, and the substantive reading was done in a real rendered browser session with the accordions expanded; its ModernGov document search is broken (control query returned a byte-identical empty form to both the real query and the nonsense control), so committee papers could not be full-text searched and the designation dates remain unfound.

E06000052.research: Cornwall is a large unitary authority so it was checked specifically for a scheme covering only a named town rather than the whole county; none was found. The HMO page states 'Any property which has 5 or more people (forming 2 or more households), where there is sharing of kitchens, WC or bathrooms will need an HMO licence' - the national mandatory test only, with no designation mentioned. MAJOR FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: Cornwall operates the 'Cornwall Responsible Landlord Scheme'. Scraped datasets frequently misclassify this as licensing because the page title contains the word 'Scheme' and it sits under private housing. It is not statutory: the council's wording is that it 'supports and encourages landlords and letting agents to provide safe, well managed and good quality accommodation', membership is voluntary, and 'There is no cost in joining the scheme'. A voluntary free accreditation scheme has no basis in Part 2 or Part 3 and confers no licence. SECOND TRAP: an HMO licence fee review consultation concerns the fee level for mandatory licences, not a designation. No evidence of any designation covering Camborne, Redruth, Penzance, Newquay or any other Cornish town.

E07000079.research: The HMO page describes only the mandatory regime, setting the test as properties 'occupied by five or more people, forming two or more households; AND tenants share facilities such as kitchen or bathrooms'. It also notes that purpose-built flats in blocks of up to two units fall within mandatory licensing on the same test. There is no reference to any s.56 or Part 3 designation. The council's supporting document is titled 'HMO Mandatory Licensing Flowchart' and its decision logic turns solely on whether there is 'rent or other consideration payable' and whether 'five or more persons, comprising 2 or more households occupy the property'; the word 'mandatory' in that filename usefully confirms the scope of the council's offer. Cotswold is a rural district with a small dispersed private rented sector and no low-demand or high-deprivation profile of the kind that supports a Part 3 designation. NOTE: the page discusses the Management of Houses in Multiple Occupation Regulations 2006, which apply to licensable and non-licensable HMOs alike; management regulations are not a licensing scheme.

E06000053.council: Council of the Isles of Scilly
E06000053.research: MANDATORY THRESHOLD ONLY: a licence is required where 'it's rented to 5 or more people who form more than 1 household' together with sharing or lack of amenities, and the building height requirement was removed on 1 October 2018. Enforcement wording: 'The Council can issue a Civil Penalty Notice upto £30,000 for offences relating to licensing and management of HMO's.' REGISTER CORROBORATION: the public register states 'This register is required under the Housing Act 2004 Part ll and shows all HMO's in the Council of the Isles of Scilly area that are currently licenced.' The register is scoped to Part 2 mandatory licensing; there is no Part 3 selective register, which s.232 would require if a selective scheme existed. SITEMAP SWEEP: the full sitemap contains ZERO occurrences of 'selective'. The private sector housing branch contains fourteen pages, none a licensing designation, and the licensing branch contains only alcohol, gambling, street trading, sex establishment and boatman licences. TRAP: the housing landing page references a 'Responsible Landlord Scheme'. This is a voluntary accreditation initiative, not a Housing Act 2004 designation. CONTEXT: the Isles of Scilly is England's smallest authority, roughly 2,200 residents, and a selective licensing designation here would be highly implausible; the site evidence is consistent with mandatory-only.

E07000226.research: The HMO page states that 'all HMOs that have five or more persons forming two or more households must be licensed', the national mandatory threshold, and makes no reference to any designation. Fees are published separately as the 'HMO licence fees and charges guide 2026 to 2027'. SIGNIFICANT FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: the same page states that 'Article 4 Directions affecting the creation of new HMOs in 10 zones across Crawley have been approved and in effect from 15 June 2022'. That is a planning measure removing permitted development rights for converting a dwellinghouse to a small HMO in those zones; it requires planning permission, not a licence. Aggregators very frequently convert a ten-zone Article 4 direction of this kind into a phantom 'additional licensing scheme covering 10 areas' complete with invented ward lists, and the 15 June 2022 date must never be recorded as a scheme start date. A democracy-portal paper titled 'Identifying and Monitoring HMOs in Crawley' discusses licensing frameworks in general terms without adopting a designation.

E07000096.research: The HMO licences page sets the licensing trigger where a property 'is occupied by five or more people' and 'has two or more households'. That is the national mandatory test and the page contains no reference to a s.56 or Part 3 designation. Mandatory fees published for 2026-2027, for context only: initial licence application £610; five year licence ongoing management £953; one year licence ongoing management £287; £25 for each additional bedroom over five rooms. TRAP: the same page warns that operating an unlicensed HMO can lead to unlimited fines, civil penalties up to £30,000 and rent repayment orders of up to twelve months' rent. Scrapers sometimes treat rent repayment order warnings as a signal of selective licensing, but these penalties attach to mandatory licensing too and prove nothing about a designation. The council's general licensing landing page covers its enforcement policy across licences and permits and lists no property licensing designation.

E06000005.research: Two independent checks on the council's own site, both negative. First, the HMO page describes only mandatory licensing, referring to the pre-2018 test and then to the 1 October 2018 extension under which 'smaller properties used as HMOs in England which house 5 people or more in 2 or more separate households will in many cases require a licence. The requirement for three of more storeys for a property to need a licence will be removed.' No designation mentioned. Second, and more probative, the published fee schedule was examined line by line: Part A licence application £217.00, 'Part B 5 year HMO licence per letting' £155.00, licence variation £124.00, HMO officer time £65.00 per hour, plus general enforcement, empty homes and immigration inspection charges. There is NO selective licence fee and NO additional licence fee anywhere in the schedule. A council operating a Part 3 designation must charge a fee for it and would publish it here, so the absence is strong corroboration. REGIONAL TRAP: neighbouring Durham County Council does operate selective licensing, and Darlington is frequently swept into County Durham in scraped geographies despite being a separate unitary authority.

E07000107.research: The HMO page states that 'Licensable HMOs are currently those of 5 or more persons in two or more households', with the standard exception that a purpose-built flat in a block of three or more self-contained flats does not require a licence, and notes that a live-in landlord needs a licence only with 'four or more lodgers/Tenants'. Mandatory fees 2025/26: £905 new five-year licence, £695 re-licence. TRAP 1: the same page sets out Article 4 style planning control with staged dates, new HMOs north of the A2 requiring planning permission from 9 December 2025 and south of the A2 from 10 December 2026. These are planning permission requirements, not licensing designations, and the geographic split by the A2 is exactly the sort of detail scrapers convert into a fake part-borough licensing scheme with a 2026 start date. TRAP 2: the council's 'Landlords Guide to the Housing Act' explains in general educational terms that 'The Council may also be able to declare that other types of HMOs will need to have a licence. This is called additional licensing', and separately describes selective licensing in the abstract. That is generic explanatory text about powers the council could use, phrased conditionally as 'may also be able to', not a declaration that a scheme exists.

W06000004.research: ACTIVE and recently expanded. The council's live page states: 'Denbighshire County Council Additional Licensing (Houses in Multiple Occupation) Scheme 2025. On the 21st October 2025, Cabinet approved the Denbighshire County Council Additional Licensing (Houses in Multiple Occupation) Scheme 2025. The areas of Denbigh, Llangollen, Prestatyn and Rhyl have been redesignated for Additional HMO Licensing and the scheme has also been expanded county wide. The scheme will commence on 1 February 2026 and will run for a maximum of five years until 31 January 2031.' The primary designation notice confirms it: 'Notice is hereby given that Denbighshire County Council has on the 21st October 2025 designated a county wide Additional Licensing Scheme... effective from 1st February 2026 and unless revoked beforehand or extended will cease to have effect on 31st January 2031', citing the Wales 2006 Regulations and the Housing Act 2004 (Additional HMO Licensing Wales) General Approval 2007, and catching s.254 HMOs with 'three or more persons, forming two or more households' plus s.257 converted flats. THE PART 2 vs PART 3 QUESTION IS SETTLED OUTRIGHT by the council's own 2025 consultation proposal: 'Section 56 Housing Act 2004 gives power to Local Authorities to designate areas of their district... as subject to additional licensing.' This is s.56, not Part 3. The council sets out the licensable test plainly: 'Under our Additional Licensing Scheme, a HMO property must have a licence if: there are three or more tenants living there AND they form more than one household, with or without shared facilities', expressly contrasted with the mandatory test of 'three or more storeys AND five or more tenants'. THE IMMEDIATE PREDECESSOR is recorded as expired: 'on the 28th day of July 2020 designated an Additional Licensing Scheme... covering the electoral wards of Denbigh, Llangollen, Prestatyn and Rhyl... effective from 1st December 2020 and... will cease to have effect on 30th November 2025.' Two earlier Rhyl-area schemes also existed (Cabinet approval 8 September 2009 expiring 31 December 2014; a second designation approved 16 December 2014), but their exact commencement dates are not published, so they are not recorded as dated records rather than asserting inferred dates. FEE-SCHEDULE TEST, decisive: licences last five years and cost by storeys and habitable rooms, with the ladder STARTING AT 'four or less' habitable rooms (£855/£655/£455 depending on storeys), below the mandatory five-occupant threshold, which is exactly the small-HMO tell of a genuine s.56 scheme. The council's own summary is 'A basic fee of £890 is worked out on the cost for 5 habitable rooms in a building of 3 or more storeys. There is an additional charge of £35 for each habitable room for properties that have between 6 and 10 habitable rooms.' There is also a separate payment route, cost code '3479-40142 (Additional Licence)' versus '3479-40091 (Mandatory Licence)', plus a £200 early-application discount and a 50 per cent charity discount. SELECTIVE LICENSING: none, ever. Zero occurrences across the 4,303-URL sitemap, the full web archive, and every designation and policy document read. WARDS NULL on both records. The 2020 notice calls Denbigh, Llangollen, Prestatyn and Rhyl 'electoral wards', but they are town names that pre-date the 2022 boundary review and do not correspond to current ONS ward names, so coverage 'areas' with wards null is used. The active scheme is county-wide, so no ward list is needed at all. TRAPS EXCLUDED: Rent Smart Wales; mandatory HMO licensing, which the page correctly separates; the West Rhyl Housing Improvement Project and the West Rhyl regeneration area, which appear only as a ward label on a private-rented-stock chart and are regeneration not designation, and which are the classic Rhyl false lead; all Welsh 'dewisol' hits on the domain, which are discretionary housing payments, discretionary business grants and elective home education; and 'anghenion dysgu ychwanegol' (additional learning needs), the dominant 'ychwanegol' false positive. LIMITATION: WebSearch was unavailable and external engines blocked scripted queries, so every finding rests on direct fetches of denbighshire.gov.uk documents; the same pages were independently located via the council's own sitemap.

N09000005.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Derry City and Strabane therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Northern Ireland district councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply NI-wide instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Private Tenancies (Northern Ireland) Order 2006 art.65A: all landlords letting under a private tenancy must register. Registration lasts 3 years and costs £70 online or £80 on paper, with a £500 fixed penalty or a court fine up to £2,500. ADMINISTRATION CHANGED RECENTLY: Councils since 1 March 2025, with Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council as lead/host council for all 11 NI councils (previously the Department for Communities). (2) HMO LICENSING under the Houses in Multiple Occupation Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 s.1: 3+ persons as only or main residence forming more than two households, rent payable by at least one. A single NIHMO Unit at Belfast City Council administers HMO licensing on behalf of all 11 NI councils, and can take enforcement action for all of them, so a landlord in Derry City and Strabane does not apply to their own council. Licences run 5 years. Statutory maximum rose from £45 to £75 per person per annum on 1 August 2025 (SR 2025/124). Belfast currently charges £62 per person per year, so £310 per person over a 5-year licence. Penalties run to a £5,000 fixed penalty and £20,000 on summary conviction. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: NARROWER THAN ENGLAND: NI requires MORE THAN TWO households (i.e. 3+). Three sharers from two households are an HMO in England but NOT in NI. PLANNING: Planning permission is also required for a new HMO; Belfast will not process a licence application without it.

E06000059.research: Dorset is a large unitary authority so it was checked specifically for a scheme limited to a named town; one was proposed for Weymouth and never designated. The council's page is titled 'Mandatory HMO licensing' and states 'Unless there is a specified exemption, all properties that meet the definition of a licensable HMO as specified in the Housing Act 2004 must possess a valid HMO licence from the local authority.' Fees from 1 April 2026: £900 for a first five year licence, £740 to renew, reduced 10 per cent to £810 and £666 for landlords meeting Council Landlord Forum standards. PRINCIPAL TRAP, and it is serious: there is a large council-hosted paper trail for a proposed selective licensing scheme in part of Melcombe Regis ward, Weymouth, including a consultation report, a consultation document, 'Draft Conditions for Selective Licensing of the Private Rented Sector in Melcombe Regis' dated October 2018, and a ModernGov committee issue titled 'Designating an area of the Melcombe Regis for Selective Licensing'. The consultation was run by the former Weymouth and Portland Borough Council, whose own wording was that it 'is considering the introduction of a Selective Licensing Scheme under the Housing Act 2004 in parts of the Melcombe Regis ward'. It was never designated, and a subsequent Dorset committee item put forward voluntary landlord accreditation and targeted enforcement as an alternative to designation. Because these documents are numerous, hosted on the council's own domain and use confident designation language, scrapers routinely record a live Weymouth scheme. There is none, and no start date should ever be published for it. ACCESS NOTE: the council domain and its ModernGov portal return HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so pages were read via a text-extraction proxy of the council's own pages, and the ModernGov issue page itself could not be opened. GEOGRAPHY TRAP: Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole is a separate unitary authority and its arrangements must not be attributed to Dorset Council.

E07000108.research: This negative is confirmed by a formal council disclosure rather than by absence of mention, which makes it unusually reliable. Freedom of information response FI16759, published in the council's disclosure log, answers a structured request about 'Property Licensing Schemes'. The council identifies exactly one scheme in operation, 'Mandatory HMO', with coverage stated as 'Whole area'. The questions relating to selective licensing and additional HMO licensing, including scheme status, confirmation references and designation details, are answered 'not applicable', because no such designations exist. TRAP: the phrase 'Whole area' describes the geographic reach of the national mandatory HMO regime, which applies everywhere by law, and scrapers reading it alongside the words 'licensing scheme' can wrongly generate a district-wide selective licensing designation. Nothing on the council's licensing pages indicates a s.56 or Part 3 designation. Landlords in Dover, Deal, Sandwich and the surrounding villages therefore need a licence only where the property is a mandatory HMO.

E08000027.research: Two separate council pages covering private rented housing were checked and both refer to mandatory HMO licensing only. The private landlords page states 'All HMOs that have five or more people in them must be licensed by the local authority. There is a fee for the licensing of each HMO', and it maintains an HMO register current as of 20 July 2026, showing the page is actively maintained. The private housing landing page states 'The Council licenses HMOs where at least 5 tenants live there, forming more than one household but share facilities like a kitchen, bathroom, and toilet'. Neither page mentions a s.56 or Part 3 designation, and the section navigation lists Private Landlords, Home Owners, Private Tenant, Private Sector Enforcement, Harassment and Illegal Eviction, Empty Properties, Dudley home improvement service, Housing Associations, and Stock Condition Survey, with no property licensing designation section. TRAP: the private housing page cites a Building Research Establishment stock condition analysis of 31 March 2020 finding that of roughly 25,000 private rented homes in Dudley 'some 16,000 will have at least one Category One Hazard'. Poor stock condition evidence of this type is the standard justification a council publishes when building a case for selective licensing, and its presence causes scrapers to infer a scheme. WEAKEST RECORD IN THIS BATCH: this is an absence-of-mention negative rather than an explicit denial, with no designation notice, cabinet decision or fee found. Re-check this one first if challenged.

S12000006.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Dumfries and Galloway therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Scottish councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply nationally instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Antisocial Behaviour etc. (Scotland) Act 2004 Part 8: all landlords must register with each council where they let (exemptions: resident landlords, holiday lets, agricultural tenancies); joint owners must all register; adverts must show the registration number. Registration lasts 3 years and costs about £85 per council plus £20 per property (no per-property fee where the property is a licensed HMO), with a £170 late fee and a maximum penalty of £50,000. (2) HMO LICENSING under the Housing (Scotland) Act 2006 Part 5 s.125: 3+ persons who are not all members of the same family or of one or other of two families (i.e. 3+ households), sharing a basic amenity, as only or main residence. Licences typically run 3 years, the fee is set by each council, and the maximum penalty is £50,000. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: Scotland's HMO test is THREE or more people from three or more households, which is broader than England's mandatory five. TRAP EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED: Enhanced Enforcement Areas (Housing (Scotland) Act 2014 ss.27-28) are area-designated but are NOT a licence; they grant extra discretionary enforcement powers only. Enhanced Enforcement Areas are the single most likely thing to be mistaken for selective licensing in Scotland, because they are area-designated and housing-related, but they confer no licence requirement on any landlord.

E07000009.research: The council's HMO licensing information page sets out a three part test and requires a licence only where the answer to all three is yes: 'Is the property occupied by 5 or more persons?', 'Do the occupants form 2 or more households?' and 'Are basic amenities shared, for example a bathroom or kitchen?'. That is precisely the national mandatory threshold, and no s.56 or Part 3 designation is mentioned. The page confirms a fee is payable but does not publish the amount; a December 2025 committee report titled 'Review of the Houses in multiple occupation (HMO) Licensing fees' concerns the level of mandatory HMO fees rather than any new designation. The council's application form is likewise a mandatory HMO form. URL TRAP: the site redirects /licensing-and-permits/ to /services/licensing-and-permits/, and development and staging hosts such as eastcambs-dev.invdev.com appear in search indexes; those are not citable council addresses. CONTENT TRAP: some third party guidance describes the licensable threshold in East Cambridgeshire as '3 or more tenants', which is the pre-2018 mandatory test and is wrong; the council's own current wording is five or more persons. East Cambridgeshire is a rural district covering Ely, Soham and Littleport with no published Part 3 designation.

E07000040.research: The HMO licensing page describes only the mandatory regime: 'properties occupied by five or more people making up two or more households', with the standard s.254 tests and the usual exemptions (s.257 HMOs, educational institutions, RSLs, religious communities). The application form page is titled 'Mandatory HMO Licence Application Form' and refers to the government 'extending the mandatory HMO licensing scheme', i.e. the 1 October 2018 national extension, not a local designation. FEE CORROBORATION: the HMO application fee page lists new licence fees as 'Up to 5 occupants = £600, 6 or more occupants = £800'. There is no fee line for a selective or additional licence anywhere in East Devon's published housing or environmental health fee schedules; the Environmental Health Licensing Fees page covers only animal licensing, skin piercing, export certificates and scrap metal. Council site search for 'selective licensing' (322 results) and 'additional licensing' (795 results) returned no page describing any such scheme; all licensing hits were alcohol, animal, zoo, scrap metal or mandatory HMO. The HMO register page states only 'Certain HMOs are subject to mandatory HMO licensing'. No false-positive traps encountered: no Article 4 direction and no licensing consultation material was found on the housing pages.

E07000085.research: The HMO page states under 'Licensing of HMO's': 'It is a statutory requirement for us to operate a licensing scheme for HMOs with five or more people, from two or more households.' That is the national mandatory threshold, described expressly as a statutory duty rather than a local designation. FEE CORROBORATION: 'Prices for council services 2026' contains only these housing licence lines: HMO Licence (5 or less occupants) 5 year licence £600.00; 6 to 10 occupants £710.00; 11 to 15 £820.00; 16 to 20 £930.00; 20+ £1,040.00. There is no selective or additional licence fee anywhere in the schedule, which is strong corroboration because any live s.56 or Part 3 scheme must carry its own cost-recovery fee. COMMITTEE PAPERS: ModernGov document search for 'selective licensing' returned 1 result and 'additional licensing' returned 1 result, both the same Licensing Committee item of 11 September 2018, 'HMO Licensing Policy'. No designation report, statutory consultation or cabinet decision to designate. SITE STRUCTURE: the full sitemap contains no selective or additional licensing page; private sector housing subsections are limited to advice for renters, advice for tenants, disabled facilities grants, empty properties, HMO, private sector housing enforcement and mobile park homes. NOTE: the council's own site search returns an unfiltered generic list and is not usable for keyword confirmation, so the negative rests on the HMO page wording, the fee schedule, the sitemap and the ModernGov search.

E07000242.research: The HMO page is unusually explicit and effectively rules itself out: 'Not all HMOs require a licence. Currently, HMOs with 5 or more occupants in 2 or more households require a licence under the Housing Act 2004. In some other districts other properties also require a licence under additional or selective licensing.' The phrase 'in some OTHER districts' distinguishes East Herts from authorities that do operate such schemes. The same page repeats: 'Landlords currently need an HMO licence in most cases if a property has five or more occupants forming more than one household.' The HMO licence application page states 'Landlords need an HMO licence if a property has five or more tenants forming more than one household' with no mention of any discretionary scheme. FEE CORROBORATION: Environmental Health Fees and Charges lists only mandatory HMO lines - New: 'HMO licence with no more than five bedrooms - Part 1' £1,157, 'Part 2' £305, full fee on application £1,432, additional bedroom £31; Renewal: Part 1 £916, Part 2 £305, full fee £1,191, additional bedroom £31. No selective or additional licensing fee. LICENCE INDEX: the 'Licences and registration' index lists 17 licence types (alcohol, taxi, HMO, animal, food premises, betting, gaming machines, lotteries, skin piercing, sex establishments, charity collections, leaflet distribution, market traders, street trading, cooling towers, mobile homes site licences, scrap metal). HMO is the only private-rented-property licence. No Article 4 direction or licensing consultation was found.

E07000137.research: The strongest negative in this batch because the council states it in writing. The South and East Lincolnshire Councils Partnership Housing Standards HMO Licensing Policy 2026-2029 says under its additional licensing heading: 'Under section 56 of the Housing Act 2004, additional licensing of HMOs covers those HMOs that are not licensed under the mandatory scheme but where the Council has used its power to designate areas of the Borough/District subject to additional licensing of HMOs. The Council do not currently operate an additional licensing scheme but maintain the right to introduce this if considered appropriate during the course of this policy.' The word 'selective' does not appear anywhere in the policy. The policy is partnership-wide, adopted across East Lindsey, South Holland and Boston. The HMO web page sets out the mandatory test only: the standard, self-contained flat or converted building test under s.254, 'The property is occupied by 5 or more people', and 'occupied by persons living in two or more separate households.' FEE CORROBORATION: the Enforcement Policy Fees and Charges appendix has a single housing licensing section headed 'HOUSES IN MULTIPLE OCCUPATION (HMO) LICENSING - Under Part 2 of the Housing Act 2004', with New Licence £300.00 initial application plus £150.00 for each unit of accommodation, renewal identical. No Part 3 selective fee and no s.56 additional fee. SITE SEARCH: council search for 'selective licensing' returns no results; 'additional licensing' returns only an unrelated large-music-event premises licence page.

(1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Antisocial Behaviour etc. (Scotland) Act 2004 Part 8: all landlords must register with each council where they let (exemptions: resident landlords, holiday lets, agricultural tenancies); joint owners must all register; adverts must show the registration number. Registration lasts 3 years and costs about £85 per council plus £20 per property (no per-property fee where the property is a licensed HMO), with a £170 late fee and a maximum penalty of £50,000. (2) HMO LICENSING under the Housing (Scotland) Act 2006 Part 5 s.125: 3+ persons who are not all members of the same family or of one or other of two families (i.e. 3+ households), sharing a basic amenity, as only or main residence. Licences typically run 3 years, the fee is set by each council, and the maximum penalty is £50,000. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: Scotland's HMO test is THREE or more people from three or more households, which is broader than England's mandatory five. TRAP EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED: Enhanced Enforcement Areas (Housing (Scotland) Act 2014 ss.27-28) are area-designated but are NOT a licence; they grant extra discretionary enforcement powers only. Enhanced Enforcement Areas are the single most likely thing to be mistaken for selective licensing in Scotland, because they are area-designated and housing-related, but they confer no licence requirement on any landlord.

E06000011.research: DELIBERATELY NOT CONFIRMED EITHER WAY, because no live-or-expired verdict could be evidenced to a safe standard. The licensing page states: 'Under the national mandatory licensing scheme the definition of an HMO which must be licensed is one that has 5 or more people, forming 2 or more households, who are sharing facilities such as toilets, bathrooms and kitchens regardless of the number of storeys.' THE GOOLE REFERENCE: the only mention of any discretionary scheme sits inside a clearly historical section headed 'What are the changes to mandatory HMO licensing from 1 October 2018?', which reads: 'If you currently have an HMO licensed under the council's additional licensing scheme which operates in Goole and it falls under the new definition of a mandatory licensable HMO, your current licence will remain valid, and no action is needed until it comes up for renewal.' That paragraph is written in 2018 tense (surrounding text says 'New rules will also come into force') and is a transitional note, not a current designation statement. EVIDENCE IT IS NO LONGER LIVE: (1) the current fee schedule on the same page, expressly 'effective from 1 April 2026', lists only mandatory HMO fees - new 1-year £510.00 for a 5-bedroom property plus £25 per additional bedroom, new 5-year £1,205.00, renewal 1-year £510.00, renewal 5-year £1,015, pre-application advice £240 inc VAT, replacement licence £45 - with no additional or selective licensing fee line; (2) there is no application route or dedicated page for an additional licence, and probes of two plausible paths both returned 404; (3) the 'Available licences' index lists 'Houses in multiple occupation' as the only property licence; (4) a s.56 designation lasts a maximum of five years, so a scheme described as operating in 2018 would have lapsed by 2023 unless redesignated, and no redesignation is published. EVIDENCE AGAINST CALLING IT EXPIRED: the council's own live page still uses the present tense 'which operates in Goole', and no revocation notice, expiry date or committee decision could be found to date the end. NO SELECTIVE LICENSING FOUND: the A-Z has no selective licensing entry and the private housing landlords section covers only HMOs, landlord training, landlord liaison, HHSRS and general advice. LIMITS: the site search is JavaScript-rendered and could not be queried server-side, and the ModernGov committee site returned HTTP 522. A landlord in Goole with a 3-4 occupant HMO or a s.257 converted building could be misled either way, so this is flagged unverified rather than given a false negative. ACTION: confirm with private.sector.housing@eastriding.gov.uk or h.licensing@eastriding.gov.uk before relying on a nil return for a Goole property.

This includes any flat which contains five or more people living in two or more households where the flat has not been purpose-built to multiple occupant standards and flats above or below commercial premises.' Mandatory test only. The page also carries a stale pre-2018 line, 'Generally speaking, this will apply to any HMO of three or more storeys that is occupied by five or more people in two or more households', still mandatory wording. POTENTIAL FALSE POSITIVE: the page ends 'All HMOs (licensable or otherwise) should also be registered with the local council.' That is an administrative or voluntary registration statement with no fee and no designation behind it; it is NOT a s.56 or Part 3 scheme. FEE CORROBORATION: the fees and charges schedule 2026/27, Housing Services section 6.1, is headed 'Houses of multiple occupancy licences' and is the only housing licensing fee in the document: new licence up to and including seven lettable units, Part A £515.85 plus Part B £714.05, total £1,229.90, additional £25.00 per unit over seven; renewal Part A £345.81 plus Part B £702.72, total £1,048.53. Searching the whole schedule for 'selective' and 'additional licensing' returns zero matches. COMMITTEE PAPERS: CMIS search for 'selective licensing' returned 8 documents, none a designation. E07000061.research: Council statement, last modified 23 July 2025, under the heading 'HMO Licensing': 'Eastbourne Borough Council currently operates a mandatory licensing scheme under the Housing Act 2004, which requires an HMO licence for any property with 5 or more unrelated occupiers living as separate households and sharing amenities.' The HMO licensing page covers application forms, prescribed standards, registers and fees, with no mention of additional licensing, selective licensing, designated areas or wards. N09000006.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Fermanagh and Omagh therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Northern Ireland district councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply NI-wide instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Private Tenancies (Northern Ireland) Order 2006 art.65A: all landlords letting under a private tenancy must register. Registration lasts 3 years and costs £70 online or £80 on paper, with a £500 fixed penalty or a court fine up to £2,500. ADMINISTRATION CHANGED RECENTLY: Councils since 1 March 2025, with Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council as lead/host council for all 11 NI councils (previously the Department for Communities). (2) HMO LICENSING under the Houses in Multiple Occupation Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 s.1: 3+ persons as only or main residence forming more than two households, rent payable by at least one. A single NIHMO Unit at Belfast City Council administers HMO licensing on behalf of all 11 NI councils, and can take enforcement action for all of them, so a landlord in Fermanagh and Omagh does not apply to their own council. Licences run 5 years. Statutory maximum rose from £45 to £75 per person per annum on 1 August 2025 (SR 2025/124). Belfast currently charges £62 per person per year, so £310 per person over a 5-year licence. Penalties run to a £5,000 fixed penalty and £20,000 on summary conviction. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: NARROWER THAN ENGLAND: NI requires MORE THAN TWO households (i.e. 3+). Three sharers from two households are an HMO in England but NOT in NI. PLANNING: Planning permission is also required for a new HMO; Belfast will not process a licence application without it.

W06000005.research: ACTIVE, brand new, and the strongest-evidenced record in this batch. INDEPENDENTLY RE-VERIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR via direct fetch: the page is headed 'Public Notice in Respect of the Introduction of an Additional Licensing Scheme for Houses of Multiple Occupation in Flintshire'. The notice itself is unambiguous: 'This designation is published in accordance with Sections 56 to 60 of the Housing Act 2004 and Regulation 9 of the Licensing and Management of Houses in Multiple Occupation and Other Houses (Miscellaneous Provisions) (Wales) Regulations 2006. Notice is hereby given that on 14th October 2025, Flintshire County Council designated an Additional Licensing scheme in respect of Houses in Multiple Occupation, which operates in accordance with the Regulations and APPLIES TO THE WHOLE COUNTY. The designation will be known as the "Flintshire County Council Additional Licensing (Houses in Multiple Occupation) Scheme 2026"... The Scheme will be effective from 1st April 2026 and unless revoked beforehand or extended will cease to have effect on 31st March 2031.' The Part 2 vs Part 3 question is settled on the face of the instrument: s.56 to 60, additional, not selective. The Welsh mirror page uses 'trwyddedu YCHWANEGOL' and never 'dewisol' or 'dethol'. SCOPE, quoted: 'The Scheme applies to all Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) within Flintshire, except those exempted by the relevant sections of the HA 2004 and those already licensed under the Mandatory Licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation Scheme. The Scheme includes properties that meet all of the criteria, within either one of the following two categories: Any type of HMO as defined by Section 254 of the Housing Act 2004 which does not fall within the mandatory licensing scheme, occupied by three or more persons, forming two or more households. HMO properties which are defined within the scope of Section 257 of the Housing Act 2004; HMO's created by converting buildings into flats, but do not meet the 1991 Building Regulations.' The notice also spells out the stakes: 'Failure to apply for a licence where required is an offence under Section 72 of the HA 2004. A person who commits an offence is liable on summary conviction to an unlimited fine... In addition, that person may be required to repay up to 12 months' rent.' FEE-SCHEDULE TEST, decisive: the live Licensing Fees and Charges table reads 'HMO Licence Application Fee (For the first 5 Units) £849.40 / HMO (Each Additional Unit) £38.79 / Service of an Enforcement Notice under the Housing Act 2004 £396.68', with the council stating 'The fee has been set on a cost recovery basis in line with government guidance and covers both application processing and inspection.' Cost recovery is the statutory hallmark of a self-financing designation. IMPORTANT FEE CAUTION: 'Units' here means letting units or rooms, NOT occupants, so this is not the five-occupant mandatory-only ladder; and the council publishes no separate mandatory-versus-additional split, so £849.40 plus £38.79 per extra unit is simply what a Flintshire HMO landlord now pays. THIS IS FLINTSHIRE'S FIRST EVER SCHEME. The October 2025 Cabinet report says it 'will bring Flintshire County Council in-line with many other counties in Wales, who have well-established licensing schemes of this sort', and only 14 mandatory HMO licences existed in September 2024. There is consequently no expired predecessor. THE CONNAH'S QUAY, SHOTTON, FLINT AND HOLYWELL ASSOCIATION IS A FALSE LEAD, checked specifically: those are Town Centre Regeneration, SHARP and Place Making programmes, not designations. The scheme is county-wide with no area carve-outs; the only geographic mention in the papers is a consultation respondent's remark about HMO concentration in Deeside. SELECTIVE LICENSING: none. Wayback CDX sweeps show no selective-licensing URL ever existed on the domain. TRAPS EXCLUDED: Rent Smart Wales; Welsh mandatory HMO licensing under WSI 2006/1712 (W.174); s.254 definitional recitals; statutory power recitals; the per-unit surcharge line, which here sits inside a genuine s.56 scheme rather than standing in for one; and Article 4 and planning permission. The s.257 coverage is NOT the England '(Additional Provisions) (England) Regulations 2007' trap, since the notice cites the Wales 2006 Regulations and s.56 directly. LIMITATIONS: Flintshire's main site search FAILED its control test (byte-identical ~27.9KB shells for 'council tax', 'zzqqxx' and the real query) and was discarded; the committee search failed as GET but worked as POST, where controls passed cleanly. There is no pre-April-2026 archive snapshot of the fee table, so it cannot be proved the £849.40 was introduced with the scheme. Note the council's own misspelling of 'Licencing' in the URL.

E07000112.research: The council states: 'All HMOs with five or more people making up two or more families will need a licence to operate. This applies regardless of their size. This is accordance with the Licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation (Prescribed Description) (England) Order 2018.' That is the national mandatory regime and the only trigger given. The register is described as 'The public register for mandatory licensed HMOs', with no separate additional or selective register. Fees: application £1,130, renewal £960, one mandatory line only. The council's own site search for 'selective licensing' returned about 14 results, every one either a generic legislative reference or unrelated. The two relevant ones are the Private Sector Housing Enforcement Policy 2021, which merely lists the statutory offence of 'Failing to licence a house subject to selective licensing under Part 3' as a category of offence the policy would cover if it applied, and the Overview and Scrutiny Committee annual report 2024-25 recording that a presentation 'reviewed private sector housing enforcement and considered a selective licensing scheme'. Considered is not designated: there is no designation notice, no scheme page, no fee and no area map.

E07000080.research: The council page carries the heading 'Mandatory HMO licensing' and describes only the national regime, including the flats-above-shops extension: 'Purpose built flats will also come within the definition, where there are up to two flats in the block and one or both of the flats are occupied by five or more persons in two or more separate households.' No selective or additional scheme is mentioned anywhere in the private housing section. Fees: application (Part 1) £240.88, licence issue (Part 2) new £1,091.63, renewal issue £989.13. WORDING TRAP: the same fee table includes 'Additional fee for seven or more rooms, £41.00 per additional letting room (capped at £400.00)'. That is a per-room surcharge on a mandatory HMO licence, not an additional licensing scheme under s.56, and must not be read as one. A sitemap sweep of 700 URLs returned no page containing 'selective' or 'additional licensing' in a housing context; the only 'additional' hit was a planning permissions page.

E07000119.research: The council page describes only the national mandatory regime and points to the Licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation (Prescribed Description) (England) Order 2018 for the full list of licensable types. The clinching evidence is the fee schedule, which labels every line as mandatory: 'HMO Mandatory Licence (Housing Act 2004) Up to Five Units: £1,107.00', 'Each Additional Unit: £45.00', 'HMO Licence Renewal (Housing Act 2004) Up to Five Units: £850.00', 'Each Additional Unit: £45.00'. There is no selective or additional licensing fee, which a live discretionary scheme would have to carry. IMPORTANT FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: searches for 'Fylde selective licensing' surface an article headed 'Selective Licensing Scheme to Improve Rented Properties'. Reading it shows it is about BLACKPOOL COUNCIL, not Fylde: 'A new Selective Licensing Scheme... in the inner area of Blackpool has been approved... It covers the eight inner wards of Bloomfield, Brunswick, Claremont, Talbot, Tyldesley, Warbreck, Waterloo and Victoria... The scheme begins on 1 April 2025', directing landlords to blackpool.gov.uk/selectivelicensing. 'Fylde Coast' is a sub-regional label covering Blackpool, Fylde and Wyre, so Blackpool's scheme is routinely and wrongly attributed to Fylde. None of those wards is in Fylde Borough.

S12000049.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Glasgow City therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Scottish councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply nationally instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Antisocial Behaviour etc. (Scotland) Act 2004 Part 8: all landlords must register with each council where they let (exemptions: resident landlords, holiday lets, agricultural tenancies); joint owners must all register; adverts must show the registration number. Registration lasts 3 years and costs about £85 per council plus £20 per property (no per-property fee where the property is a licensed HMO), with a £170 late fee and a maximum penalty of £50,000. (2) HMO LICENSING under the Housing (Scotland) Act 2006 Part 5 s.125: 3+ persons who are not all members of the same family or of one or other of two families (i.e. 3+ households), sharing a basic amenity, as only or main residence. Licences typically run 3 years, the fee is set by each council, and the maximum penalty is £50,000. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: Scotland's HMO test is THREE or more people from three or more households, which is broader than England's mandatory five. TRAP EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED: Enhanced Enforcement Areas (Housing (Scotland) Act 2014 ss.27-28) are area-designated but are NOT a licence; they grant extra discretionary enforcement powers only. Enhanced Enforcement Areas are the single most likely thing to be mistaken for selective licensing in Scotland, because they are area-designated and housing-related, but they confer no licence requirement on any landlord.

E07000088.research: The council states the licence trigger as the national mandatory test only: 'An HMO licence is required if all of the following apply: It has five or more occupiers comprising two or more separate households, regardless of number of storeys...' and confirms 'From 1 October 2018, mandatory licensing is no longer limited to HMOs that are three or more storeys high'. Neither 'selective licensing' nor 'additional licensing' appears. The private rented landing page lists only three items: Private tenants, the RAPS scheme, and Renters Rights Act. TRAP CHECK: RAPS (Rented Accommodation in the Private Sector) is a voluntary landlord accreditation scheme, not a licensing designation. A full sitemap sweep of 1,153 URLs returned no URL containing 'selective' or 'additional licensing'. SECOND TRAP CHECK: the council published a consultation on 23 July 2026, 'Have your say on new policies to protect private renters in Gosport'. Reading it confirms it is NOT a licensing consultation: it seeks views on a Private Rented Sector Housing Enforcement Policy and a Renters' Rights Act Civil Penalty Policy, running to 11 September 2026. No licensing designation is proposed. Fareham and Gosport share a regulatory service and both HMO pages are mandatory-only in identical terms.

E07000109.research: Checked with extra care. The HMO page states 'If a HMO fits A. The Standard Test, or B. The Self-contained flat test, or C. The Converted building test and it has five or more people living there, and those in occupation make up more than one household (family unit), the property must have a HMO licence', under the heading 'Mandatory licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation'. The fee page gives a single HMO fee split in two parts: new Part A £541.81 and Part B £463.81; renewal Part A £464.98 and Part B £444.93. Relevant legislation is listed as the Housing Act 2004, the 2006 Miscellaneous Provisions Regulations and the 2018 Prescribed Description Order, mandatory only. No selective or additional fee line exists. The Private sector housing index and the Licensing index each list Houses in Multiple Occupation as the only housing licence, and a sitemap sweep returned zero URLs containing 'selective' or 'additional licensing'. DECISIVE COUNCIL STATEMENT: a council news item, 'Gravesham Borough Council seeks to extend powers over HMOs', says plainly 'The council operates the national mandatory HMO licensing scheme', reports 107 licensed HMOs at the end of March 2026, and explains that Cabinet 'agreed to continue work towards the adoption of an Article 4 Direction which would see all such conversions requiring planning permission'. FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: estate agent and aggregator pages market a 'Gravesend 2026 selective licensing health check' and postcode checkers. There is no council designation, no fee and no area behind these. The genuine 2026 development is an Article 4 planning direction, which is excluded.

E07000209.research: The council gives an explicit negative for additional licensing. Under 'When a licence is not needed' it states 'If there are three or four unrelated tenants living in the property that share facilities, this is still a HMO. This property will not need a HMO licence from us.' Under an additional licensing designation those very properties would need a licence, so that sentence rules one out. Fee £1,037.34, with a £25 discount for landlord-organisation members and £50 for Guildford Letting Scheme accredited landlords. One fee line only. The Housing licences index lists only an HMO licence and a caravan site licence. COMMITTEE EVIDENCE: the Cabinet report 'Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMO) Update', 19 April 2021, has a section '18. Alternative Controls: Additional Licensing and Article 4' recording that these were 'previously considered by the 2014 Overview and Scrutiny task and finish group. In 2014, the provisions were noted as being Inappropriate to Guildford's set of circumstances at that time.' It reports that 'Currently the data suggest that unlicensable HMOs that would meet the definition of an Additionally Licensed HMO are not being significantly mismanaged', and describes an additional scheme only conditionally: 'A proportion of the Council Tax data set of 1,800 student HMOs that currently do not require a licence, would need a licence to operate, if an Additional HMO Licensing Scheme was brought into force.' A committee minute separately records that 'Guildford Borough had mandatory HMO licensing only and that HMOs of 3-4 persons did not require a licence to operate lawfully.' Considered, never designated.

W06000002.research: THE HARDEST CALL IN THIS BATCH, so the reasoning is set out in full. The scheme unquestionably EXISTS and is county-wide s.56 additional licensing. INDEPENDENTLY RE-VERIFIED BY THE COORDINATOR via direct fetch, which confirmed the page still reads: 'Additional licence - For all other HMOs Cyngor Gwynedd has decided to make the additional licence relevant to all of Gwynedd to maintain standards. The fee for this licence is £160 per unit in addition to a £50 fee to process the application.' The Welsh page is identical in substance. The statutory public notice linked from that page confirms the power and the dates: 'This notice is published in accordance with Sections 56 to 60 of the Housing Act 2004 and Regulation 9 of the Licensing and Management of Houses in Multiple Occupation and Other Houses (Miscellaneous Provisions)(Wales) Regulations 2006... The designation applies to the whole area of the County of Gwynedd... The designation was made by the Cabinet Member for Housing on the 21.05.2021... The designation will be effective from 04.06.2021 and unless revoked beforehand will CEASE TO HAVE EFFECT ON THE 03.06.2026.' WHY IT IS RECORDED AS EXPIRED: today is 5 August 2026, so the only designation instrument Gwynedd publishes lapsed roughly two months ago, and no re-designation could be found. A companion Revocation Notice on the same page does NOT kill this scheme; it revokes the PREDECESSOR scheme effective 04.06.2021 under Reg 10, reason given 'Designation of a new additional licensing scheme... from the 04.06.2021'. That was checked specifically, because a revocation notice sitting beside a live scheme is an obvious trap. Gwynedd has therefore run rolling county-wide additional licensing for years. WHY THIS IS FLAGGED RATHER THAN TREATED AS SETTLED: the council UPDATED BOTH LANGUAGE VERSIONS OF THE PAGE ON 11 JUNE 2026, after expiry, and still presents the additional licence as current and still quotes its fee. Weighing that: the PDF internal timestamps show both notices were merely re-saved on 09.06.2026 against 2021 creation dates, consistent with the bulk CMS migration that moved /en/ paths to /en-gb/ rather than a substantive update; the asset-library copy is byte-identical by MD5; Wayback holds only one snapshot (2022) with a different digest, so there is no history to diff; and six plausible new-notice filenames under both document paths all returned 404. Gwynedd's ModernGov was searched across 30 meetings of Cabinet and Communities Scrutiny for January 2025 to October 2026 with zero matches for trwydd, licen, amlddeiliad, HMO, dewisol or ychwanegol; that scan is CONTROL-VALIDATED, since the same parser extracts real agenda items from Cabinet on 9 June 2026. HOWEVER the 2021 designation was made by the Cabinet Member individually rather than by Cabinet, and Gwynedd's officer and member decisions register returned 'No matching decisions' for every date range tried, which is not trustworthy. So a renewal by delegated decision is plausible and could not be excluded. Because the harm of under-warning is severe (s.72(1) carries an unlimited fine plus a rent repayment order), the public note deliberately tells landlords the council is still advertising and charging for the licence and to check before letting, rather than implying they are clear. FEE-SCHEDULE TEST: passed strongly. A distinct additional-licence fee of £160 per unit plus £50 processing is published in both languages, precisely the separate cost-recovery signal a genuine s.56 scheme must carry. SELECTIVE LICENSING: none exists or has been proposed. TRAPS EXCLUDED: Rent Smart Wales; mandatory 3-storey/5-person licensing under WSI 2006/1712 (W.174), which the page keeps expressly separate; Article 4 directions and second-home planning policy; Gwynedd's high second-home and empty-home council tax premiums, which are tax not licensing and are a strong local distractor; the s.254 definition; and the Welsh homonyms 'taliadau-tai-dewisol-dhp' (Discretionary Housing Payments) and 'tai-gofal-ychwanegol' (Extra Care Housing). LIMITATIONS, all control-tested: ModernGov mgDelegatedDecisions ignores TitleContains; ieSearchResults 404s on POST and returns byte-identical responses for the control, the nonsense query and the real query; and the site search reports '1024 results' for the nonsense control exactly as for 'council tax'. None of those nil results is relied on. A direct call to Gwynedd's Private Rented Sector Unit is the one step that would close this gap and no automated route could substitute for it.

E06000006.research: Direct council statement, given twice on the private housing page: 'Local authorities have the discretionary power to introduce additional or selective licensing in relation to private rental properties or smaller Houses in Multiple Occupation. To date Halton Council has not introduced additional or selective licensing in any areas of the borough.' The same page describes only 'Mandatory HMO Licensing - A House in Multiple Occupation with 5 or more tenants must by law be licensed by the local authority.' LIVE PROPOSAL, not a designation: a separate page is headed 'Consultation on a Selective Licensing Scheme for Privately Rented Homes' and states 'Halton Borough Council is proposing to introduce a Selective Licensing scheme under Part 3 of the Housing Act 2004. If approved, the scheme would require most privately rented homes in the proposed designation areas to be licensed by the Council, unless exempt by law.' Consultation dates 'from Monday 3rd August at 12pm to Sunday 18th October 2026 at 11.59pm'. The page confirms the statutory position that 'Before introducing a Selective Licensing scheme, the law requires the Council to carry out public consultation', and that the consultation covers 'The proposed licence fee and payment arrangements', so no fee is yet set. Recorded with status 'proposed' rather than omitted, because landlords in the named wards need to know a decision is imminent. TRAP: the council page notes 'In areas of the borough where the article 4 direction applies planning permission must be obtained to convert a dwelling house to a smaller HMO'. Planning control, excluded. RE-CHECK SCHEDULED: after 18 October 2026.

E07000131.research: The council states the trigger as the national mandatory test only: 'Some HMOs (not Section 257s) require a licence. A property needs a licence if it has 5 or more people who form more than 1 household (ie not all from 1 family)', with the standard exemption 'A purpose-built flat situated in a block comprising three or more self-contained flats is not subject to mandatory licensing even if that flat is an HMO.' No reference to selective or additional licensing. CORROBORATION from the council's own list of every licence it issues: the only housing entry is 'Apply for a house in multiple occupation licence'. There is no selective or additional licence application, which a designated scheme would require. NOTE ON LIMITS: the council's site search and its fees and charges page were intermittently unavailable ('Harborough DC is temporarily offline for scheduled routine maintenance') during checking, so a per-line fee schedule could not be read. This does not affect the conclusion, which rests on the licence trigger wording and the complete list of licences issued, but the fee page is worth a re-check.

E07000073.research: Checked with extra care. The live council page describes only the national mandatory test: 'Your property will need a mandatory licence if: it is rented to 5 people or more who form more than 1 household; some or all tenants share toilet, bathroom or kitchen facilities.' Its fee schedule has a single line: 'Mandatory licence for 5 or more occupants: £850 (reduced £600)', plus £80 per bedroom above six. No selective or additional fee. The register is 'the mandatory licence HMO public register', and the public register page offers only that plus temporary exemption notices. DIRECT POLICY STATEMENT: the Private Sector Housing Enforcement Policy, under the heading 'Selective licensing', states 'The Housing Act 2004 allows for the introduction of selective licensing schemes and additional licensing schemes. These are not currently considered appropriate to be adopted within Harlow, but this matter will be kept under review.' The document records 'This policy was last updated on 14 July 2023. The next review date is 13 March 2029', so it is current. FUTURE INTENTION, NOT A DESIGNATION: the corporate policy 'Building Harlow's Future', the main corporate framework for 2026 to 2027, includes the commitment 'Introduce a selective licensing scheme for private rented homes across Harlow.' That is an aspiration with no consultation, no designation notice, no confirmed area, no start date and no fee, so it is not recorded as a scheme, but landlords should watch for a statutory consultation. FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: the HMO page states applicants 'must have full planning permission to convert your property to a HMO - this applies to all applications because of a town-wide HMO Article 4 direction'. A town-wide Article 4 direction is planning control, not licensing.

E07000089.research: The council states 'You may have to apply to us for a licence if you rent out a property as a house in multiple occupation to five or more people', the national mandatory threshold and the only trigger given. The published fee table is decisive because its lowest band is the mandatory threshold: 'Licence for 5 persons £893; Licence 6-10 persons £1,121; Licence 11-15 persons £1,344; Licence 16-20 persons £1,565; Licence 21+ persons £1,786', with renewals from £686. There is no fee band for three or four occupiers, which an additional licensing designation would require, and no selective licensing fee for ordinary private lets. Neither 'selective licensing' nor 'additional licensing' appears anywhere in the private sector housing section, and a sweep of 833 sitemap URLs returned no such page. TRAP CHECK: the 'How we work with landlords' page describes a rent deposit and letting incentive scheme where the council 'act as a free letting agent' for its clients. That is a voluntary landlord incentive service, not a licensing designation.

E07000090.research: The only property-licensing page frames the scheme purely as the national statutory duty: 'It is a statutory requirement for us to operate a licensing scheme for HMOs with five or more people, from two or more households - as of October 2018'. FEE CORROBORATION: the same page carries the complete published fee list and every line is a mandatory occupancy band with no discretionary line: 5 occupants £817.09; 6-10 £873.66; 11-15 £984.64; 16-20 £1,302.34; 20+ at an additional hourly rate, for a 5-year licence. SITE SEARCH: a search for 'selective licensing' returned 'Your search yielded no results.' A search for 'additional licensing' returned five results, none about property licensing (hackney carriage drivers, the mandatory HMO page, club premises certificates, knowledge test, keeping primates). SUPPORTING: the private sector housing hub links to six sub-pages, none a discretionary scheme; the licensing A-Z lists only alcohol, gaming, hackney carriage and 'other licences and permits' with no property licensing category. TRAP: the phrase 'we operate a licensing scheme' reads like a discretionary designation but is explicitly the national mandatory duty from October 2018. CAVEAT: Havant publishes no explicit denial; the finding rests on convergent absence across the HMO page, fee schedule, housing hub, licensing A-Z and two site searches.

E06000019.research: The licensing directory entry describes the mandatory threshold only: 'any property that is let to five people or more, in two separate households, who share either bathroom or cooking facilities, will now require to be licenced', effective 1 October 2018, removing the previous three-storey test. FEE CORROBORATION: a basic application fee for a 5-year licence of £1,404 from 1 April 2026, with a 5% discount for accredited landlords and 15% for renewals, stackable to 25%. One fee stream only; no discretionary licensing fee line. SITE SEARCH: 'selective licensing' returned 3 results, none relevant. TRAP, IMPORTANT: a search for 'additional licensing private rented' surfaced a committee decision 'REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION OF HEREFORDSHIRE AMENITY STANDARDS' citing the 'Multiple Occupation (Additional Provisions) (England) Regulations 2007'. That is the HMO amenity and space standards regulation, NOT Part 2 s.56 additional licensing. Any keyword matcher combining 'additional' plus 'licensing' plus 'HMO' would false-positive here. SUPPORTING: the housing hub's Landlords section contains only three items (HMO licensing, the landlord account, the deposit/bond scheme) and the landlord advice page covers HHSRS and enforcement with no licensing scheme. CAVEAT: no explicit council disclaimer exists.

E07000098.research: The HMO licensing page sets the requirement as 'Which properties need licensing? ... Properties occupied by five or more people in two or more households', the plain mandatory threshold with no lowered trigger. FEE CORROBORATION: 'New and renewal applications Up to five people £1,306.00'; 'Every additional person over five £105.00'; variation £366.00. Only mandatory fee lines exist. MAJOR TRAP IDENTIFIED AND EXCLUDED: 'The Hertsmere Borough Council (Houses in Multiple Occupation) (Potters Bar) Article 4 Direction 2026'. This is a PLANNING Article 4 Direction, not licensing. The council's own wording: 'An Article 4 Direction is a legal mechanism used by local authorities that removes permitted development rights.' It addresses planning Use Class conversions from C3 to C4. It is a non-immediate direction made 23 April 2026, consulted 6 May to 17 June 2026, and 'will come into force on 06 May 2027, if confirmed'. It names four wards: Potters Bar Parkfield, Potters Bar Oakmere, Potters Bar Furzefield, Bentley Heath and The Royds. Because it names wards AND carries three dates AND is dated in the future, it is the single most dangerous false positive in this batch and could easily be miscoded as an 'upcoming' licensing scheme. SECOND TRAP: a news item on 'proposed amenity standards for houses in multiple occupation' concerns amenity and space standards, not a designation. SITE SEARCH: the working parameter is '?term='; a search for 'selective licensing' returns one result, 'Apply for a Film Classification'. The full sitemap contains zero occurrences of 'selective'. SUPPORTING: the private sector housing hub lists eight pages under Housing Enforcement, none a discretionary scheme.

E07000037.research: The HMO page describes the mandatory scheme only: 'any property that is let to 5 or more unrelated persons who are living as two or more separate households and who share either bathroom or cooking facilities will now require to be licenced by the Local Authority'. FEE CORROBORATION: first application £450.00 for five years; renewal £350.00; change of licence holder £350.00. No discretionary fee line. Non-compliance carries 'a civil penalty up to £30,000 or, if prosecuted, an unlimited fine'. Licensing is run by the Private Sector Housing Service with no geographic limitation. STRONGEST NEGATIVE: the dedicated Private rented homes page sets out landlord obligations at length, covering the Renters' Rights Act 2025, deposit protection, energy efficiency standards and letting agent redress, and contains no licensing or registration requirement of any kind. A live selective scheme would necessarily be flagged there. SUPPORTING: the landlord hub links only to HMO, empty properties, private rented homes, empty-home reuse, enforcement, grant assistance and registered providers; the enforcement page covers empty-property powers with no licensing scheme. CAVEAT STATED PLAINLY: the site search endpoint could not be located, with several patterns returning 404, so no keyword sweep was possible. This is evidentially the weakest negative in this batch, though the topic pages and fee schedule are consistent.

E07000132.research: This council gives the clearest wording in the batch and the closest thing to an explicit disclaimer: 'you don't need a licence to rent out all HMOs in the borough of Hinckley and Bosworth'.
