E07000202.research: Checked with particular care and verified twice independently, both passes agreeing. THRESHOLD IS UNAMBIGUOUSLY MANDATORY, WITH A DATE: 'From 1st October 2018, it is mandatory for landlords of Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) occupied by five or more people from different households to obtain an HMO licence'. FEE CORROBORATION: 'The full licence fee for a House in Multiple Occupation is £155 per unit of accommodation', payable in two parts since 1 October 2020. No discretionary licensing fee line. Note the page also carries a stale worked example that does not reconcile at £155/unit; treat £155/unit as the headline. SITE SEARCH AND SITEMAP: a search for 'selective licensing' returns 'Your search yielded no results.' The full sitemap contains ZERO occurrences of 'selective'. LICENCE A-Z: lists sex establishments, skips, building control, skin piercing, industrial licences, mobile/park home licence, HMO licence (described as 'mandatory HMO licensing requirements') and pleasure boat licences. DECISION REGISTER: the delegated decisions register covering 7 August 2020 to 6 August 2026 contains no selective or additional licensing designation and no consultation authorisation. A Part 3 designation is a formal executive decision and would necessarily appear. CONSULTATIONS: no selective-licensing consultation, current or closed; the only licensing item is a closed alcohol Cumulative Impact Assessment. TRAP 1, ALMOST CERTAINLY THE SOURCE OF ANY 'IPSWICH HAS SELECTIVE LICENSING' CLAIM: an Article 4 Direction in force 1 June 2024 covering 12 wards (Alexandra, Bixley, Bridge, Castle Hill, Gainsborough, Gipping, Holywells, Priory Heath, Rushmere, St John's, St Margaret's, Westgate), which 'removes existing permitted development rights for material changes of use from dwelling houses (C3 use class) to small houses of multiple occupation (C4 use class)'. In that area planning permission is required for HMOs with three or more unrelated individuals. Planning control, NOT licensing, and routinely misreported as 'Ipswich licenses 3+ HMOs'. TRAP 2: the HMO landing page carries loose wording implying three or more people requires a licence; that is the s.254 definition with the licensing caveat elided. LIMIT: the ModernGov keyword endpoint is POST/JS-driven and the decisions register begins August 2020, so a pre-2020 abandoned consultation cannot be fully excluded.

W06000001.research: NEGATIVE, triangulated four ways. The council's HMO page states verbatim: 'Licensing is mandatory for all HMOs which have three or more storeys and are occupied by five or more persons forming two or more households.' The Welsh page matches. That is the mandatory threshold only, with no 'all other HMOs' extension of the kind Gwynedd publishes next door. The full page was read in raw HTML and contains ZERO occurrences of 'additional licen', 'selective licen', 'ychwanegol' or 'dewisol'. The council's own public register is titled 'Register of mandatory houses in multiple occupation licences', the word 'mandatory' being the council's own, and there is no parallel additional-licence register. FEE-SCHEDULE TEST, decisive: Anglesey's live 'Council fees and charges from 1 April 2026' schedule, a 51-page document, contains exactly three HMO lines: 'Houses in Multiple Occupation MANDATORY Licence Application Fee £749.00'; 'Houses in Multiple Occupation MANDATORY Licence Renewal Fee £557.50'; 'Houses in Multiple Occupation Public Register £64.50'. There is no additional-licensing fee and no selective-licensing fee anywhere in the 51 pages, and a live scheme must be self-financing. All 39 occurrences of 'additional' in that document were checked and every one is an unrelated surcharge, the classic false positive. Zero occurrences of 'selective'. SITEMAP SWEEP: all 2,523 URLs parsed and grepped raw for 'selectiv', 'dewisol', 'ychwanegol', 'trwydd', 'HMO' and 'amlfeddiannaeth'. No licensing-scheme page exists, and Anglesey's licences-and-permits tree has no housing or residential licence branch at all, unlike Gwynedd's; HMO work sits under environmental health. TRAPS EXCLUDED AND NAMED: Rent Smart Wales, for which Anglesey has two dedicated pages and to which the HMO page directs landlords at its close, the dominant Welsh false positive; the s.254 definitional paragraphs, which run to four bullet descriptions on this page; the linked gov.wales tenant guidance whose anchor text reads 'councils... have powers to require licensing of other HMOs', a statutory-powers recital describing the power not its exercise; the £64.50 public-register fee, which is s.232 cost recovery for supplying a copy of the register and is NOT a licensing fee; council tax premiums on second and empty homes, a major local issue but tax not licensing; Article 4 and conservation-area planning rules; and the Welsh homonyms 'Anghenion Dysgu Ychwanegol', 'Rhyddhad dewisol', 'Thaliadau Tai Dewisol', 'Addysg ddewisol yn y cartref' and 'Rheolau cynllunio ychwanegol', which together account for every single 'dewisol' and 'ychwanegol' hit on the domain. REACHABILITY: no 403s encountered; anglesey.gov.wales redirects to anglesey.gov.uk, which serves canonical content on both /en/ and /cy/ paths.

E06000046.research: ACCESS NOTE, IMPORTANT FOR REPEAT RUNS: iow.gov.uk returns HTTP 403 to automated fetchers because its robots.txt explicitly disallows AI crawlers including ClaudeBot and GPTBot. Plain curl with a standard browser user-agent returns HTTP 200 normally. This council is therefore VERIFIED, not unverified; the 403 is a bot block and carries no information about licensing. Every finding was re-run and independently confirmed by direct curl. THE COUNCIL'S OWN SEARCH INDEX IS THE PRIMARY EVIDENCE, and it indexes PDFs as well as pages (it surfaces corporate plans and consultation PDFs), so a nil return is meaningful: a search for 'selective licensing' returns verbatim 'Searching on "selective licensing" found no results'. A search for 'property licensing' returns 'found no results'. TRAP: a search for 'additional licensing' returns one result, and that single hit is a planning consultation PDF about great crested newt DISTRICT LICENSING, an ecology matter with no connection to housing. A search for 'licensing scheme' returns 6 results, all the same newt district licensing scheme plus Corporate Plan PDFs. Any keyword matcher on 'additional licensing' would false-positive on the newt documents here. HMO PAGE: 'A house in multiple occupancy is one property with three or more tenants, who are a part of more than one household (not family), that share a toilet, bathroom, or kitchen. A large HMO has five or more tenants.' The 'three or more' figure is the s.254 statutory DEFINITION, not a licensing threshold. EVIDENTIAL WEAKNESS STATED PLAINLY: the fee-schedule test CANNOT be applied here, because the council publishes no HMO fee schedule at all, directing enquiries to a phone number, and its general licensing fees page contains zero occurrences of HMO, houses in multiple, housing or selective. The negative rests on the zero-result search index plus the mandatory-only HMO page. RESIDUAL RISK: ModernGov committee papers were not exhaustively read.

E06000010.research: HIGH PRIORITY council, verified twice independently, both passes agreeing. MANDATORY THRESHOLD ONLY: 'A property is classed as an HMO subject to licensing if it is occupied by 5 or more persons. These persons form 2 or more households, and they share a bathroom or kitchen.' FEE CORROBORATION, strongest evidence: fees are listed by bedroom count only, from 3 bed at '£225 + £629.50' up to 10 bed at '£225 + £823.75', plus '£27.75 per additional bedroom'. There is no selective or additional licensing fee line anywhere. Note the bands starting at 3 bedrooms reflect property size, not occupancy, and are consistent with mandatory-only since a 3-bedroom property can house 5 people. SITEMAP SWEEP: the full sitemap contains no URL matching selective or additional licensing, and direct probes of two plausible selective-licensing paths returned 404. LANDLORD AND TENANT HUBS BOTH SILENT: neither lists any licensing scheme, and the tenant hub lists 20 topics with no mention of licensed areas. A live scheme would have to be signposted to tenants as well as landlords. REGISTER: cites only s.232 and lists no designated wards, areas or streets. TRAP 1: the Hull Accredited Landlord Scheme appears prominently and reads like a scheme, but 'You can apply to join', i.e. voluntary accreditation, not a designation. TRAP 2: the HMO application page refers to 'an additional licensing fee invoice', meaning an extra fee, NOT Part 2 s.56. TRAP 3: Hull operates 27 Article 4 Directions and one is explicitly 'Houses in Multiple Occupation'. Planning control removing permitted development rights, in the council's own words: 'in some areas, mainly conservation areas, we have removed some of these rights by making Article 4 Directions.' HISTORICAL GAP STATED PLAINLY: Hull was flagged as historically operating selective licensing. No past designation could be confirmed or dated; there is no expired-scheme page, archive note or designation notice reachable on the domain, the site search returned 404 on every pattern tried, and the committee system failed with a TLS certificate error. The confident finding is that NO scheme is live now; historical dates are unverifiable and are not asserted.

E08000034.research: PRIMARY SOURCES READ IN FULL, all council-owned. (1) The live HMO page states the licensing trigger as 'A property rented to 5 or more people who form more than 1 household' where 'some or all tenants share toilet, bathroom or kitchen facilities' - the national mandatory threshold, with no designation, wards or dates. (2) FEE SCHEDULE, mandatory bands only: 5-6 bed spaces £664; 7-8 £764; 9+ £882; 'A licence will normally last for a maximum of five years'. No selective or additional fee line, which a live scheme would need to be enforceable. (3) The statutory public register says 'Kirklees Council keeps a register of all licences that have been issued to operate Houses in Multiple Occupation' and scopes it to properties let to '5 or more separate tenants not in the same family group'. A discretionary scheme would require its own register entries. (4) The full housing index was enumerated link by link: HMO, HMO register, landlord accreditation, guide to renting privately, Renters' Rights Act, report repairs. No discretionary licensing page. (5) The Private Sector Housing Assistance Policy (October 2025) was read in full and contains no selective or additional licensing provision. (6) A search of democracy.kirklees.gov.uk for 'selective licensing' returned no results, so no cabinet or committee report proposes a scheme. TRAPS: a legacy landlord booklet carries headed sections 'Additional licensing of HMOs' and 'Selective licensing' that look like announcements but are generic 2006-era recitals of the statutory powers, and the same document concludes 'Kirklees Council, initially intends to implement mandatory licensing and to continue to work with landlords... through the accreditation scheme.' Aggregators also publish a 'Selective licensing in Kirklees: streets, fees, postcode check' page, which is not a council source. ON THE DEPRIVATION POINT: Kirklees plainly has areas that would support a case for selective licensing, but the council has not made one; its published choice is accreditation plus enforcement.

E08000011.research: PRIMARY SOURCES READ IN FULL, all council-owned. (1) The council's own licence-need test states: 'A landlord must have a licence for a privately rented HMO if the property being rented out: is occupied by five or more people; those people form two or more households; tenants share some amenities like kitchen, bathroom or laundry'. That is the national mandatory threshold and nothing beyond it. If a selective scheme were designated, ordinary private rented homes in the designated area would need a licence and this page could not be written that way. (2) FEE SCHEDULE 2026-2027, mandatory HMO only: five-year licences £875 (5 persons) rising to £1,880 (16+ persons); one-year £420 to £731; plus accommodation certificate and Part 1 enforcement at full cost recovery. No discretionary licensing fee. (3) The housing index enumerated in full: empty homes, energy efficiency, homelessness, Homes for Ukraine, HMO, housing strategies, housing support, Renters' Rights Act, TESS. No discretionary licensing page. (4) The council's complete licence register enumerates taxi and private hire, animal, leisure and personal treatment, business and street trading, gambling, child employment, and alcohol and entertainment, with no housing licence at all. (5) The A-Z was pulled for letters S and L: no selective licensing entry and no landlord licensing entry. TWO TRAPS, both material here: (a) the landlord guidance page carries the passages 'Additional licencing of HMOs is a discretionary power that Councils may decide to apply...' and 'This is where the Council may declare that certain areas, for example, where there is low demand for housing and/or antisocial behaviour, are appropriate for selective licencing.' Conditional recitals of the statutory powers, with no area, dates or fee. (b) The customer portal hosts a 'Selective Licensing' presentation given to the Private Landlord Forum in July 2013 and consultation material from November 2012, including survey findings. That is a historic consultation that did not result in a designation. ON THE DEPRIVATION POINT: Knowsley did actively explore selective licensing in 2012-13 and did not proceed, which is consistent with the negative finding.

E07000121.research: The highest-risk council in this batch, settled on the official minutes rather than a secondary report. PRIMARY SOURCE, the statutory record: Cabinet minutes of 16 April 2024, published 18 April 2024, effective 26 April 2024. Minute 99, 'Review of the Consultation on Landlord Licensing and the enforcement of housing standards in the West End of Morecambe', set out three options: 'Option 1: Do nothing'; 'Option 2: Introduce a selective landlord licensing scheme in the West End of Morecambe'; 'Option 3: Update an alternative enforcement approach, build on landlord and tenant engagement and explore the introduction of a Good Landlord Charter.' The minutes record 'The officer preferred option is option 3'. On a recorded vote of 8 to 1, Cabinet RESOLVED: '(1) That Cabinet notes the outcome of the public consultation... (2) That Cabinet agrees to not implementing landlord licensing at this time from this consultation, but to concentrate on a more intelligence led, targeted enforcement approach. (3) That approval be given to co-develop and agree to the introduction of a Good Landlords Charter. (4) That Cabinet agrees to the commissioning of a full stock condition survey... (5) That approval be given to the development of an action plan...' Option 2 was rejected and no designation was made. CORROBORATION: the Private Landlords Newsletter fifth edition (July 2023) confirms the consultation covered 'the West End and Heysham North areas of Morecambe', notes 'A previous consultation for a selective and additional licensing scheme was held in 2017 where the decision was to pause implementation... in favour of a targeted enforcement approach', and states plainly under 'Current property licensing schemes in Lancaster District': 'Lancaster City Council operates the mandatory licensing scheme as this is the national scheme required by the Housing Act 2004.' The seventh edition (May 2024) reports the same decision to landlords. FEE SCHEDULE from April 2026, read in full: new five-year licence £156 application plus £602 licence, £758 total for a five person HMO, plus £57 per extra person; renewal £654; maximum £1,600; £114 discount for accredited landlords. Mandatory only, no discretionary line. The private rented accommodation index lists ten sub-pages with no licensing scheme page; /selective-licensing returns 404. Recorded as no scheme rather than 'proposed' because the consultation closed and was refused. NOTE the wording 'at this time from this consultation' leaves the door open, so Lancaster is worth re-checking. Historic: Cabinet on 8 August 2017 had approved developing a Morecambe scheme and consulting, which was then paused.

E07000063.research: Backed by a direct council statement. The published FOI response (FOI 14362 'Mandatory HMO') answers whether the council 'only has the Mandatory HMO licensing scheme in place at this current time'. Under 'Response by Lewes District Council' it says: 'Yes, just the mandatory scheme' and 'Additional or selective licensing is not required in LDC, therefore no consultations were carried out. LDC has a very small number of HMO's'. Asked for 'any live and up and coming designations and with a map of coverage area', the answer is 'N/A'. CURRENCY CHECK, since the FOI is not recent: the HMO page (last modified 13 May 2026) offers a single licence route covering 'HMO's in Eastbourne borough and the Lewes district'. The 'HMO License Fee Schedule 2026-2027' was read in full: Shared House 5 persons £1,140 new and £799 renewal, rising to £1,213 at 9 persons; Bedsit £1,283 to £1,573; Hostel £1,140 up to £2,943 for 81+ persons; plus immigration inspection £150, pre-application advice £185, missed appointment £100, unlicensed HMO inspection £350, paper form £50, late application £50. It confirms 'As shared houses are licensed for 5 or more occupants' and frames refunds solely around 'a licence under Part 2 of the Housing Act 2004'. A text search of the whole PDF for 'selective', 'additional licen', 'part 3', 's.56' and 'designat' returned zero matches. THREE TRAPS on this shared site, all avoided: (1) a news item 'Council takes action to limit HMO conversions' is EASTBOURNE Borough, and is an Article 4 planning Direction covering 'Devonshire, Meads and Upperton wards, and a small part of St Anthony's ward' from 30 July. Named wards plus a hard date make it look exactly like a designation; it is neither licensing nor Lewes. (2) Pages titled 'Selective area housing licences - 1350' and 'Selective housing areas - 1349' rank top on the council's own search but are records-retention schedule entries carrying 'Retention Period Years 6' and 'Legislation Name: Limitation Act 1980 (Section 2)'. This boilerplate appears on many council sites regardless of any scheme. (3) The shared democracy site's HMO papers are Eastbourne's, not Lewes'. Exact-phrase searches returned 7 hits for 'selective licensing' and 14 for 'additional licensing', every one being that boilerplate, the FOI itself, Eastbourne planning material, Licensing Act 2003 policy, or the title of the HMO Management Regulations 2007.

E07000194.research: The HMO licence page states the trigger as mandatory only: 'If you are the owner/manager of a house in multiple occupation (HMO) that is rented out to five or more people, who form two or more families, and who share facilities such as a bathroom, kitchen, sink or toilet, you must get an HMO licence.' FEE SCHEDULE, HMO lines only: 'Licence fee £850'; 'Plus cost per bedroom above 5 £75', capped at £5,000; 'Renewal licence fee £850'; 'HMO immigration inspection £220'. No discretionary licensing fee line. The licensing index enumerates alcohol and event, street trading, animal, taxi, pavement, gambling, charitable collections, sex shop, caravan and residential site, scrap metal and special treatments plus HMO, with no discretionary housing scheme. A crawl of 295 housing and licensing pages found zero occurrences of the word 'selective' anywhere, and zero occurrences of 'additional licensing' used as a scheme. TWO TRAPS, both material: (1) MODEL-FORM BOILERPLATE. The downloadable HMO application form (June 2019) carries the line 'ONLY COMPLETE THIS APPLICATION FORM FOR A LICENSABLE HOUSE IN MULTIPLE OCCUPATION, WHICH INCLUDES MANDATORY LICENSING AND ADDITIONAL LICENSING.' Standard national model-form wording covering both regimes; there is no designation notice, coverage area, dates or additional licensing fee. (2) PROPOSAL-STAGE WORDING. The 'Housing, homelessness and rough sleeping delivery plan 2025-2026' contains the action 'Research benefits of additional/selective licensing approach for particular neighbourhoods and adopt if need arises', status 'Not started'. Aspiration, not a consultation and not a designation, so no 'proposed' scheme is recorded. It is a genuine forward signal though: of these twelve, Lichfield is the most likely to designate in future. LIMITATION: the site IP-blocked automated access partway through, so the sweep covered housing, licensing, homelessness, environmental health and community sections rather than all 4,013 URLs; committee papers were not inspected.

E07000138.research: PRIMARY SOURCES READ IN FULL, which matters because Lincoln is a student city where additional licensing would be unsurprising. (1) The HMO page states 'An HMO must have a licence if it is occupied by 5 or more people' - the national mandatory threshold, with no lower threshold and no designated area. (2) FEE SCHEDULE, the decisive document: 'Government regulations came into force in October 2018 that require Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) with five or more tenants to be licensed by the council'; 'Basic fee (up to 5 bedrooms) New application £1470'; renewal £1270; '6 to 10 bedrooms - Basic fee + 10%'; '11 to 15 bedrooms - Basic fee + 20%'; '16 to 20 bedrooms - Basic fee + 30%'; Trusted Landlord Scheme discount £100; 60 per cent payable on application and 40 per cent on grant. One fee structure, tied to the mandatory regime. An additional licensing scheme covering small student HMOs, the scheme type one would expect here, would require its own fee line and there is none. (3) The HMO section index contains exactly three items: Complying with the Law, HMO Article 4 Formal Process, and Houses in Multiple Occupation. (4) The Private Housing index lists ten items with no discretionary licensing page. (5) The landlord compliance page covers tenancy agreements, EPCs, gas safety, deposit protection and electrical safety, imposing no licensing obligation beyond the mandatory regime. THREE TRAPS: (a) THE BIG ONE. Lincoln operates a city-wide Article 4 Direction: 'On 1st March 2016 the City of Lincoln Council introduced an Article 4 Direction' removing permitted development rights for 'the change of use from a use falling within Class C3 (dwelling houses)... to a use falling within Class C4 (houses in multiple occupation)' across 'the City of Lincoln'. It has a commencement date and district-wide coverage and is frequently mistaken for licensing. Planning control, never a scheme. (b) The council's 'Mandatory Licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation' document recites 'Offences in relation to the Selective Licensing of houses [s95 Housing Act...]' inside a boilerplate list of civil penalty offences. (c) NAME COLLISION, and it is severe: North East Lincolnshire Council and North Lincolnshire Council both run genuine selective licensing schemes and dominate search results for 'Lincoln selective licensing', while Boston Borough Council launched a consultation on a town-wide additional licensing scheme in March 2026. All three are separate Lincolnshire authorities and none is City of Lincoln.

N09000007.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Lisburn and Castlereagh therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Northern Ireland district councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply NI-wide instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Private Tenancies (Northern Ireland) Order 2006 art.65A: all landlords letting under a private tenancy must register. Registration lasts 3 years and costs £70 online or £80 on paper, with a £500 fixed penalty or a court fine up to £2,500. ADMINISTRATION CHANGED RECENTLY: Councils since 1 March 2025, with Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council as lead/host council for all 11 NI councils (previously the Department for Communities). (2) HMO LICENSING under the Houses in Multiple Occupation Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 s.1: 3+ persons as only or main residence forming more than two households, rent payable by at least one. A single NIHMO Unit at Belfast City Council administers HMO licensing on behalf of all 11 NI councils, and can take enforcement action for all of them, so a landlord in Lisburn and Castlereagh does not apply to their own council. Licences run 5 years. Statutory maximum rose from £45 to £75 per person per annum on 1 August 2025 (SR 2025/124). Belfast currently charges £62 per person per year, so £310 per person over a 5-year licence. Penalties run to a £5,000 fixed penalty and £20,000 on summary conviction. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: NARROWER THAN ENGLAND: NI requires MORE THAN TWO households (i.e. 3+). Three sharers from two households are an HMO in England but NOT in NI. PLANNING: Planning permission is also required for a new HMO; Belfast will not process a licence application without it.

E09000006.research: Confirmed with an explicit and recent statement from the council itself, the strongest evidence in this batch. The landlord page states under 'HMO licensing': 'An HMO will require a licence from the local authority if it is: Occupied by 5 or more tenants, 4 or more if there is a live-in landlord, in 2 or more households; There is at least 1 kitchen, bathroom or toilet shared by the tenants.' Mandatory only; 'selective' and 'additional licensing' were tested for programmatically and are absent. DECISIVE: a council press release dated 25 March 2026 quotes Councillor Angela Page, Executive Councillor for Public Protection and Enforcement: 'It is important to be clear that the council cannot use HMO licensing to control where HMOs are situated, nor determine whether a property operates as an HMO.' The same release states: 'Already the council has used its planning powers in 2022 to ensure that all proposed HMOs require planning permission, using an Article 4 directive, and where HMOs are established mandatory licensing regulate the minimum standards of the property.' That is a contemporaneous, named-member confirmation that Bromley relies on mandatory licensing plus planning control and operates no discretionary designation. TRAP 1, high risk: Bromley's borough-wide Article 4 Direction made in 2022 removes permitted development rights for C3-to-C4 HMO conversions. It is planning control under the General Permitted Development Order, not a Housing Act 2004 designation. Because many London boroughs genuinely do run selective or additional licensing, Bromley's Article 4 is among the most common false positives in scraped London data. TRAP 2: the landlord page cites 'The Licensing and Management of Houses in Multiple Occupation (Additional Provisions) (England) Regulations 2007' for s.257 converted blocks; the word 'Additional' there refers to additional management provisions, not additional licensing under s.56.

E07000110.research: Independently verified twice, by two separate research passes reaching the same primary document. Maidstone actively considered additional licensing and declined it. The Cabinet decision 'Houses in Multiple Occupation Proposals', 19 March 2025, records: 'MBC has previously considered creating an Additional Licensing Scheme for smaller HMOs (of 4 persons or less), but its Housing Standards Team have felt that existing enforcement powers (through Housing Standards, Community Safety and Environmental Health) are adequate to address any issues. They remain of this opinion.' It adds that 'it would be prudent to see how this Bill progresses as it will deliver additional powers over rented properties, so allowing the Council to continue to focus licencing on larger HMOs.' The resolutions adopted were to pursue an HMO Supplementary Planning Document and to review the W1, W2 and W4 Controlled Residents Parking Zones. No scheme was designated and selective licensing was never proposed. The live HMO page gives mandatory criteria only, at least five people not all one household sharing facilities, and a single fee: 'The total cost of the application is £930. For accredited landlords, it's £895.' The Housing Strategy refers only to the statutory regime: 'We are active in ensuring those HMOs that fall within the statutory licensing scheme meet the requirements of the regulations.' A crawl of all 875 reachable pages found zero occurrences of 'selective licensing' or 'additional licensing'; 27 pages returned a JavaScript challenge and were checked individually, none licensing-related. TRAP: the same Cabinet paper expresses a desire for an Article 4 Direction for HMOs and gives ward-level HMO concentrations (High Street 167, Fant and Oakwood 129). Planning and statistical, not designations, and the resulting SPD and parking zones name specific areas without being licensing. Because the March 2025 decision was a settled refusal rather than a live consultation, no 'proposed' scheme is recorded.

E07000074.research: Maldon gives the clearest negative wording in the batch. The HMO service page states: 'You are required to obtain a licence from this Authority if the property is: rented to five or more people who form more than one household; and tenants share toilet, bathroom or kitchen facilities.' It then says explicitly: 'Please note an HMO occupied by 3 or 4 unrelated individuals is not licensable because fewer than 5 persons reside at the property. There are still legal requirements applicable to such properties.' That sentence is decisive. Additional licensing is precisely the mechanism that makes small HMOs of 3 or 4 occupants licensable, so a council cannot say they are not licensable while operating one; and selective licensing would extend licensing further still, to ordinary private rented homes. Both are excluded by the council's own words. FEE SCHEDULE, 'Environmental Fees from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027': across the entire schedule there is exactly ONE housing licence line, 'House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) | Up to 5 habitable rooms | Per extra room - New £1,099 Renewal £758 £61'. Every other line is animal, food, piercing, sex establishment, caravan and camping, private water or scrap metal. STRUCTURAL CORROBORATION: the complete A-Z of council services was enumerated across all 26 letters, 212 services. It contains exactly one housing licence, 'Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMO) Licence'. There is no entry under S for selective licensing and none under L or A for additional or landlord licensing. The public register is described as 'Properties that are currently licensed with the Maldon District Council', with no separate discretionary register, and licences are 'valid for 5 years'. The Essex-wide approved Code of Practice and Essex HMO Amenity Standards are a county collaboration on standards, not a designation. TRAP: searches for Maldon HMO licensing surface Epping Forest, Chelmsford and Colchester documents; separate Essex authorities, not used as evidence.

E07000235.research: The HMO page describes an HMO as a property where 'at least 3 tenants live there, forming more than one household' sharing facilities, and states the licensing requirement arises where 'you rent a property to five or more people, not from the same household' - the national mandatory threshold. No designation, ward list or scheme wording appears. FEE SCHEDULE 2026-2027, published on the HMO page, mandatory lines only: standard licence single application £893.00 and multiple £764.00; increased occupancy 11-15 £1,454.00 / £1,387.00; 16-20 £1,454.00 / £1,387.00; 21+ £1,662.00 / £1,598.00; renewal single £653.00 and multiple £587.00, rising by band to £1,485.00 / £1,419.00. No discretionary licensing fee anywhere in the table. CORROBORATION: the Licensing index enumerates every licence type the council administers - Alcohol and Entertainment, Lotteries and Gambling, Taxis and Private Hire, Street Trading, Charitable Collections, Busking, Skin Piercing, Animal Licences, Sex Establishments, Scrap Metal, Caravan Site Licence, Pavement Licences - and contains no housing licence. The housing index lists only HMO, caravan licensing, empty homes and the Empty Homes Hub. The all-services index has no discretionary licensing entry. SHARED SERVICE NOTE: Malvern Hills shares services with Wychavon under South Worcestershire, but the HMO page gives Malvern Hills' own Private Sector Housing Team contact and Wychavon is a separate designating authority in any case. LIMITATION: the site search is JavaScript-driven and ignores URL query parameters, returning 'Results: 0' regardless of the term, so a site-search negative could not be obtained and was correctly not treated as evidence; committee papers were not inspected.

E07000133.research: Note the correct domain is melton.gov.uk; meltonbc.gov.uk does not resolve. The HMO page states: 'If you are a landlord or manager of a HMO will be required to hold a licence if the property has: Five or more occupants. More than two households.' The national mandatory threshold and nothing further; no designated area, ward, street or date. N09000008.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Mid and East Antrim therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Northern Ireland district councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply NI-wide instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Private Tenancies (Northern Ireland) Order 2006 art.65A: all landlords letting under a private tenancy must register. Registration lasts 3 years and costs £70 online or £80 on paper, with a £500 fixed penalty or a court fine up to £2,500. ADMINISTRATION CHANGED RECENTLY: Councils since 1 March 2025, with Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council as lead/host council for all 11 NI councils (previously the Department for Communities). (2) HMO LICENSING under the Houses in Multiple Occupation Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 s.1: 3+ persons as only or main residence forming more than two households, rent payable by at least one. A single NIHMO Unit at Belfast City Council administers HMO licensing on behalf of all 11 NI councils, and can take enforcement action for all of them, so a landlord in Mid and East Antrim does not apply to their own council. Licences run 5 years. Statutory maximum rose from £45 to £75 per person per annum on 1 August 2025 (SR 2025/124). Belfast currently charges £62 per person per year, so £310 per person over a 5-year licence. Penalties run to a £5,000 fixed penalty and £20,000 on summary conviction. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: NARROWER THAN ENGLAND: NI requires MORE THAN TWO households (i.e. 3+). Three sharers from two households are an HMO in England but NOT in NI. PLANNING: Planning permission is also required for a new HMO; Belfast will not process a licence application without it.

The national mandatory threshold only. FEE SCHEDULE 2026/27, the council's complete locally-set fee list: HMO Licensing new licence 3-5 units £814.00 Part 1 plus £269.00 Part 2 equals £1,083.00; 6-10 units £904.00 plus £269.00 equals £1,173.00; 11+ units £993.00 plus £269.00 equals £1,262.00; renewal 3-5 units £615.00, 6-10 £660.00, 11+ £705.00; public register requests £6.00 electronic and £9.00 hardcopy; enforcement actions £687.00 each; immigration housing visits £429.00; works in default at cost plus officer time plus a £170 admin fee. The same policy states at section 1.4 that 'Mid Devon currently has 23 licenced HMOs', consistent with mandatory-only licensing in a rural district, and no licensed non-HMO stock is referenced anywhere. Site searches for 'selective licensing' and 'additional licensing HMO' returned only that policy and the HMO Guidelines 2020, with no designation documents. LIMITATION: the council's search self-describes as covering 'our most popular pages' only, so it is not an exhaustive index; committee papers were not inspected.

S12000019.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. W06000012.research: A GENUINE PART 3 SELECTIVE DESIGNATION EXISTED HERE AND HAS EXPIRED. NO s.56 SCHEME EVER. NOTHING LIVE TODAY. THIS FINDING DISPROVES THE WORKING ASSUMPTION THAT NO PART 3 DESIGNATION HAS EVER BEEN MADE IN WALES. DESIGNATION MADE, VERIFIED VERBATIM from the primary minutes: Social Care, Health and Housing Cabinet Board, 30 January 2009, item 6, 'PROPOSED SELECTIVE LICENSING SCHEME IN THE AREA'. The minutes were downloaded and text-extracted directly. They record a DECISION, not merely a proposal: 'That, with effect from the 5th May, 2009 the area of Aberavon shown on the plan attached to the circulated report, be designated as subject to selective licensing pursuant to Section 80(1) of the Housing Act 2004; That the designation, as set out in Paragraph 1 above, cease to have effect on the 4th May, 2014 unless otherwise revoked in the proper manner under Section 88(4) of the Housing Act 2004; That the Principal Officer Environmental Health publish Notice of the making of the above designation, in accordance with the statutory requirements; That the Principal Officer Environmental Health be authorised to manage a Licensing Scheme for houses in the said area pursuant to this designation... That the above designation be kept under review... under Section 84 of the Housing Act 2004'. s.80(1) is the Part 3 designation power and s.88(4) the duration provision, so the statutory basis is unambiguous. Prior consultation was authorised on 6 Nov 2007. IT OPERATED: the Environmental Health enforcement policies of 17/03/2011, 04/04/2013 and 13/03/2014 each state 'The Environmental Health Service operates a selective licensing scheme within the county borough to address problems associated with high numbers of private rented properties and increased levels of antisocial behaviour. Landlords must obtain a license.' A March 2014 Renewal Area report records 'Selective Licensing for landlords introduced into the White City area of Aberavon to tackle high levels of ASB, high level of private rented properties (over 40%) and high levels of vacant properties.' IT LAPSED AND WAS NOT RENEWED: the June 2018 Enforcement Policy reproduces the SAME boilerplate paragraph with the selective licensing sentence DELETED, leaving only: 'The service also operates a Mandatory Licensing Scheme to regulate high risk houses in multiple occupation (HMOs), of 3 or more storeys occupied by 5 or more people not of the same family. Further powers are available should the authority decide to utilise them for the control of 2 storey HMOs.' A paged sweep of the ModernGov archive for the exact phrases 'White City' and 'selective licensing' returns NOTHING dated after 13/03/2014. FEE-SCHEDULE TEST, DECISIVE FOR THE POSITION TODAY: the environmental health fees page has a table headed 'Housing in multiple occupation licensing schemes' / 'Statutory Fees' containing exactly ONE licence fee, 'Licence of 3 Storey + £718.97', plus 'HMO Consultation Fee £77.48'. There is NO selective, NO additional, NO flat per-property and NO two-storey HMO fee. A live self-financing scheme could not exist without one. SITE SWEEP: the HTML sitemap (1,557 links) contains exactly one HMO item. Zero pages matching 'selectiv', 'dewisol', 'ychwanegol' or 'amlfedd'. The consultations page lists no licensing consultation, so there is nothing to record as proposed. TRAPS EXCLUDED BY NAME: (1) RENT SMART WALES. (2) STATUTORY-POWERS RECITAL: 'Further powers are available should the authority decide to utilise them for the control of 2 storey HMOs' describes the s.56 power as expressly UNEXERCISED, and is the single most likely source of a false positive here. (3) THE CARAVAN-SITE FEE LADDER on the same fees page ('Number of units: 5-10 £355.56, 11-20 £414.81') is Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act licensing, checked in context so it was not mistaken for a s.56 cost-recovery ladder. (4) ModernGov OR-matching noise. WARDS: deliberately null. The designation is defined by a named area shown on a plan, inside Aberavon, so coverage is 'areas' and NO WARD LIST HAS BEEN SYNTHESISED. The designation also predates the major Welsh ward boundary changes at the May 2022 elections, so any ward name carried over would very likely be stale. LIMITATIONS: NPT's website search is Google Custom Search rendered client-side and its nils prove nothing; the 1,557-link HTML sitemap was used instead. By contrast NPT's ModernGov search PASSED both controls, so its post-2014 silence IS evidence. No published fee was found for the 2009-2014 scheme, so feeApprox is null rather than guessed.

The Private housing page describes only the national scheme: 'From 1 October 2018, the mandatory licensable HMO definition has been varied to 5 or more unrelated persons who form 2 or more households.' One fee line, mandatory HMO only, with no separate selective or additional charge. No designation notice found on the council domain.

E07000175.research: The HMO licensing page states: 'The Housing Act 2004 introduced a mandatory licensing scheme for larger HMOs to improve controls and conditions within these high risk dwellings.' Corroborated by the private landlord advice page: 'There are a number of specific requirements for landlords operating houses of multiple occupation and a mandatory licensing scheme for particular high risk properties.' Again mandatory only. METHOD NOTE: the council's own site search could not be used as evidence because it is broken; a search for 'HMO' returns an empty results region even though the term certainly exists on the site, so a nil return there proves nothing and was disregarded. The 'Landlord strategy' document in the sitemap was checked and concerns the council's role as a social landlord ('This document shows what we want from our social housing'), not private rented sector licensing. The sitemap of 1,599 URLs contains no selective or additional licensing page.

E07000195.research: CURRENT POSITION: the HMO licences page describes only the national scheme, 'If an HMO has 5 or more occupiers, it is a licensable HMO and the landlord must apply for a licence.' FEE-SCHEDULE TEST: the Costs section publishes a single line, 'Licence fee (for up to five bedrooms): £750' and 'Fee for each extra bedroom: £11'. No selective or additional fee line exists. The council site search for 'selective licensing' returns 'Results 1 - 4 of about 4', and all four are the mandatory HMO licensing pages and the general Licences and registration index, none a designation. HISTORIC PROPOSALS, NOT DESIGNATIONS: the ModernGov document search returns items only from 2014-2016: Cabinet 02/04/2014 and 23/07/2014 'Proposal for Selective Licensing' for the Galleys Bank estate in Kidsgrove; Cabinet 11/11/2015 'Proposal for Selective Licensing' for the Miners Estate in Kidsgrove; and Cabinet 20/01/2016 'Selective Licensing'. The January 2016 report (wards affected: Kidsgrove) recommended only '(b) Subject to a peer review by another local authority, to agree moving forward to a ten week consultation of local residents, landlord's, businesses and other stakeholders.' That is a decision to consult, not a designation. No later document, confirmation report, commencement date or fee ever appears; the trail stops in 2016 and the scheme is absent from the live site and current fee schedule ten years on. Not recorded as 'proposed', because a 2016 consultation decision with no subsequent step would mislead a landlord into thinking a live consultation is running. TRAP EXCLUDED: the Civil Financial Penalty Policy 2026 (Cabinet 17/03/2026) contains 'Offences in relation to the Selective Licensing of `houses' [s95 Housing Act 2004]', the standard statutory civil-penalty schedule every council reproduces. TRAP EXCLUDED: the HMO page carries 'We have a number of Article 4 directions within the borough which remove some permitted development rights', which is planning control, not licensing.

W06000022.research: ACTIVE s.56 ADDITIONAL LICENSING, CITY-WIDE. THE SEALED DESIGNATION WAS VERIFIED VERBATIM by downloading and extracting the council's own PDF, linked from its additional licensing page. It reads: 'NEWPORT CITY COUNCIL HOUSES IN MULTIPLE OCCUPATION LICENSING SCHEME 2024. Newport City Council of the Civic Centre Newport NP20 4UR in exercise of their powers under Section 56 of the Housing Act 2004 hereby make the following Scheme. CITATION, COMMENCEMENT AND REVOCATION 1.1 This scheme may be cited as the Newport City Council Houses in Multiple Occupation Licensing Scheme 2024 and is made pursuant to Section 56 of the Housing Act 2004 and the Housing Act 2004 (Additional HMO Licensing) (Wales) General Approval 2007. 1.2 This scheme shall come into force on the 13th February 2025 and shall cease to have effect on the 12th February 2030 (unless revoked beforehand). 1.3 This Scheme replaces the Newport City Council Houses in Multiple Occupation Licensing Scheme 2019 which expired on the 30th of June 2024.' AREA, clause 3: 'This Scheme shall apply to all wards of the City of Newport.' APPLICATION, clause 4: 'This Scheme shall apply to all HMOs (other than those which fall within the mandatory licensing regime) which house three or more persons forming more than two single households.' FEE-SCHEDULE TEST PASSED DECISIVELY: the council's HMO licensing application advice document, fee schedule footer-dated '1st April 26', sets out two columns, 'Smaller HMOs (3-5 units/households)' and 'Larger HMOs (6+ units/households)': 'New/Initial application £1,439.78 | £78.70 extra per unit/household (maximum £1,991.84); Renewal application before expiration £1,073.87; Renewal application after expiration £1,358.29; Application following revocation of previous licence £1,073.87. Licence Variations: Property inspection required £122.69. Cancellation Charge £35.08.' THE LADDER STARTS AT THREE UNITS, NOT FIVE. A mandatory-only authority's ladder starts at five occupiers, so a dedicated cost-recovery band for sub-mandatory 3-5 person HMOs is exactly the tell of a genuine s.56 scheme, and it corroborates clause 4. THE GAP IS REAL AND MATTERS: the 2019 scheme expired 30 June 2024 and the 2024 scheme did not commence until 13 February 2025, so for that period no additional licensing was in force in Newport. Any historic liability question falling in that window must not be answered from the current designation. NO SELECTIVE LICENSING: the full sitemap was swept (an index of two pages, 3,108 URLs) and grepped for 'selectiv' and 'dewisol'. ZERO hits in either language. The only HMO URLs are the eight pages under the HMO branch. WARDS: the designation says 'all wards of the City of Newport', so coverage is borough-wide with wards null. This is the safe encoding: it avoids enumerating ward names, so the major Welsh ward boundary changes at the May 2022 elections cannot break matching. TRAPS EXCLUDED BY NAME: (1) RENT SMART WALES, which applies to every Newport landlord regardless; the s.56 finding rests solely on the sealed designation and the fee schedule. (2) PLANNING: 'Under the Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987, shared houses with 3 or more occupiers need planning consent' is planning control, never licensing. (3) The s.254 DEFINITION in clause 2. (4) CIVIL-PENALTY BOILERPLATE about s.72(1), which appears regardless of any designation. THE PREDECESSOR RECORD: the 2019 scheme is recorded as expired because the 2024 designation names it and its expiry date explicitly. The 2019 designation itself was NOT retrieved, so its start date is null and its stated area is not independently verified; it is encoded as borough-wide only because it is the direct predecessor the 2024 city-wide scheme 'replaces', and that inference is flagged here rather than presented as verified fact. Only the 30 June 2024 expiry is directly quoted from a primary source.

N09000010.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Newry, Mourne and Down therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Northern Ireland district councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply NI-wide instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Private Tenancies (Northern Ireland) Order 2006 art.65A: all landlords letting under a private tenancy must register. Registration lasts 3 years and costs £70 online or £80 on paper, with a £500 fixed penalty or a court fine up to £2,500. ADMINISTRATION CHANGED RECENTLY: Councils since 1 March 2025, with Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council as lead/host council for all 11 NI councils (previously the Department for Communities). (2) HMO LICENSING under the Houses in Multiple Occupation Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 s.1: 3+ persons as only or main residence forming more than two households, rent payable by at least one. A single NIHMO Unit at Belfast City Council administers HMO licensing on behalf of all 11 NI councils, and can take enforcement action for all of them, so a landlord in Newry, Mourne and Down does not apply to their own council. Licences run 5 years. Statutory maximum rose from £45 to £75 per person per annum on 1 August 2025 (SR 2025/124). Belfast currently charges £62 per person per year, so £310 per person over a 5-year licence. Penalties run to a £5,000 fixed penalty and £20,000 on summary conviction. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: NARROWER THAN ENGLAND: NI requires MORE THAN TWO households (i.e. 3+). Three sharers from two households are an HMO in England but NOT in NI. PLANNING: Planning permission is also required for a new HMO; Belfast will not process a licence application without it.

S12000021.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). North Ayrshire therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Scottish councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply nationally instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Antisocial Behaviour etc. (Scotland) Act 2004 Part 8: all landlords must register with each council where they let (exemptions: resident landlords, holiday lets, agricultural tenancies); joint owners must all register; adverts must show the registration number. Registration lasts 3 years and costs about £85 per council plus £20 per property (no per-property fee where the property is a licensed HMO), with a £170 late fee and a maximum penalty of £50,000. (2) HMO LICENSING under the Housing (Scotland) Act 2006 Part 5 s.125: 3+ persons who are not all members of the same family or of one or other of two families (i.e. 3+ households), sharing a basic amenity, as only or main residence. Licences typically run 3 years, the fee is set by each council, and the maximum penalty is £50,000. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: Scotland's HMO test is THREE or more people from three or more households, which is broader than England's mandatory five. TRAP EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED: Enhanced Enforcement Areas (Housing (Scotland) Act 2014 ss.27-28) are area-designated but are NOT a licence; they grant extra discretionary enforcement powers only. Enhanced Enforcement Areas are the single most likely thing to be mistaken for selective licensing in Scotland, because they are area-designated and housing-related, but they confer no licence requirement on any landlord.

E07000043.research: FEE-SCHEDULE TEST, the strongest evidence here. The current statutory fee document, 'Environmental Health and Housing Services Fees & Charges 26-27', was downloaded and converted to text in full. Section 3.11 'Houses in Multiple Occupancy (HMO)' is headed 'Housing Act 2004' and contains only mandatory unit-count bands: HMO New applications 1-5 / 6-10 / 11-15 / 16+ (Part A £530.64 to £648.56, Part B £1,023.57) and HMO Renewal applications on the same bands, plus 'Fee for copy of full HMO Licensing Register = £29.48'. A grep of the entire document for 'selective' returns zero matches. There is no selective and no additional licensing fee line anywhere in the schedule, so neither scheme can be operating. TRAP EXCLUDED: the schedule contains the strings 'Large Venues - Additional Fees', 'an additional fee', 'additional fees that may apply' and 'Additional fee for operating without a permit'. These are surcharges on events, permits and criminal record disclosure, not Part 2 s.56 additional licensing. The HMO information page has a single licensing heading, 'Mandatory licensing', explaining the post-October-2018 national scheme. METHOD NOTE: the council's Drupal site search returns fuzzy OR matches, returning unrelated harbour and land-charges pages for the query, so it was not relied on either way.

E07000038.research: The council site search gives an unambiguous negative: a search for 'selective licensing' returns 'Found 0 results. Assuming selective is required, and licensing is required, no results were found.' FEE-SCHEDULE TEST: the HMO page publishes one licence fee only, 'There is an initial application fee of £496 with a further fee when the licence is granted of £111 making a total HMO licence fee of £607 (we are under a legal obligation to split the fee).' CHECKED FOR FALSE NEGATIVE: a search for 'additional licensing' returns 27 results, but every one is unrelated licensing: the Licensing Act 2003 Statement of Licensing Principles 2024-2029, Gambling Act 2005 statements, the Draft Animal Welfare Licensing Policy 2026, and four Taxi Licensing Policy documents. E07000147.research: The council site search gives a clean negative: a search for 'selective licensing' returns 'No results found for search term selective licensing.' FEE-SCHEDULE TEST: the HMO page publishes a single licence fee, 'The Council charges £930 to licence an HMO of up to six units of accommodation for five years. For larger properties, an additional fee of £30 will be charged for every additional unit of accommodation.' One mandatory fee line, with no selective or additional scheme charge. E06000061.research: DEFINITIVE COUNCIL STATEMENT on the council's 'The law on HMOs' page, last updated 22 October 2025, under a heading 'Selective and additional licensing'. On selective: 'We currently do not meet the threshold for selective licensing as we do not have "a significant and persistent problem caused by anti-social behaviour". There is no proven link at present between ASB and HMOs, so we cannot justify selective licensing.' On additional: 'We also do not meet the threshold for additional licensing where "the local authority believes that a significant proportion of HMOs are poorly managed" - so it would not be an appropriate scheme for North Northamptonshire at the present time.' The same page confirms the only licensing in force is the national one: 'HMO licensing is a national scheme - it isn't subject to local consultation under the Housing Act 2004' and 'we are duty bound to licence any HMO on receipt of a valid HMO application under the Housing Act 2004.' No consultation is under way on either power. TRAP EXCLUDED, AND THIS IS THE KEY RISK ON THIS COUNCIL: the same page states 'An Article 4 direction came into force on 24 April 2024 for new HMOs in the Kingswood ward of Corby - this means landlords need to get planning permission for a new HMO in this area but it doesn't limit the number of HMOs', and describes six 'hotspot wards' identified by planning research in 2022/23. Article 4 is planning control over HMO conversion, carries a named ward and a commencement date, and is frequently mistaken for a licensing designation. The council itself separates the two, discussing Article 4 and then stating the licensing thresholds are not met.

E06000024.research: FEE-SCHEDULE TEST, the strongest evidence here. The council's current 'Fees and Charges 2026' document (3.7MB) was downloaded and converted to text in full. The only housing licensing entries are headed 'HMO licensing - Mandatory' (properties containing up to five units of accommodation, plus additional fee for each unit thereafter, £752.10; fit and proper persons assessment £67.75) and 'HMO Licensing - Mandatory (discounted)' (up to 5 units £599.50, each additional unit £54.55). The council has explicitly labelled these Mandatory. A grep of the whole document for 'selective' returns zero matches and for 'additional licen' returns zero matches. Since a live Part 3 or s.56 scheme must carry its own cost-recovery fee, and none exists, neither scheme is running. Corroborated by the council site search: a search for 'selective licensing' returns 'Your search yielded no results.', and the same search for 'additional licensing' also returns 'Your search yielded no results.' The HMO licensing page refers only to 'mandatory HMO licensing' when describing the offence of failing to licence. TRAP EXCLUDED: the phrase 'plus additional fee for each unit thereafter' in the schedule is a per-unit surcharge on the mandatory fee, not Part 2 s.56.

E08000022.research: DECISIVE PRIMARY SOURCE: North Tyneside's Private Sector Housing Plan 2023-2028, Appendix 1 (2024-25 Delivery Programme), lists as a future action 'Keep under review the need for selective and additional licensing in the borough'. A council keeping under review the NEED for both regimes does not operate either. The same appendix shows what it did instead: 'Introduce a landlord accreditation scheme, initially focussing on Wallsend regeneration area'. FEE TEST: the live HMO page states 'If you rent out a home to five or more people from two or more families, you might need a House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) licence from us' and its fee table reads 'HMO Application Fee: 450 / HMO Licence Fee up to 5 Units: 300 / Additional Licence Fee (per unit above 5): 32 / Change of Managing Agent: 250 / Amendment of Licence: 50'. Mandatory bands only, no Part 3 or s.56 line. NAVIGATION TEST: the Private Sector Housing hub lists only safe warm and healthy homes, empty and derelict properties, advice and support, enforcement, leaseholder information and multiple occupancy homes. /selective-licensing and /housing/private-sector-housing/selective-licensing both return 404. TRAPS EXCLUDED: (1) 'Additional Licence Fee (per unit above 5): 32' is a per-unit surcharge on a mandatory licence, NOT s.56. This is the single most misleading line on the site. (2) Landlord accreditation is explicitly labelled 'Voluntary scheme for North Tyneside landlords'. (3) The page also recites the s.254 definition (three or more people from two or more households) while the licensable threshold on the same page is five or more. (4) Neighbour bleed guarded against: nothing from Newcastle upon Tyne, which does have schemes, was used. LIMITATIONS, stated honestly: North Tyneside's sitewide search is broken, returning 'Cannot search on a disabled index', so its nil return proves nothing and carried no weight. There is no sitemap.xml (404 on all variants; robots.txt declares none), so the full-URL sweep used on other councils was impossible. The ModernGov document search ignores GET parameters, returning byte-identical 11,892-byte responses for 'selective licensing' and for the control 'houses in multiple occupation', so committee papers could not be full-text searched. The finding rests on the council's own plan wording plus the fee schedule and navigation. This is the thinnest record in batch 10: solid, but not bulletproof.

E07000218.research: COUNCIL SELF-DECLARATION. The HMO Article 4 Report to the Planning and Development Board, 6 October 2025, section 6, contains a comparator table whose North Warwickshire row reads: 29 HMO licences, 27,580 households, 0.44 licensed HMOs per 1000 population, 'Additional Scheme: No', 'Selective Licensing: No'. That is the council stating its own position in a published committee paper. FEE TEST: the HMO page states 'You need a mandatory HMO licence if: five or more unrelated people live at the property and all or some of them share a toilet, bathroom or kitchen' and 'HMO licences are usually granted for five years.' The fee table is headed 'Mandatory HMO licence Fees': New Application 5-9 £904, 10-14 £952, 15-19 £1000, 20+ £1046; Renewal £833 / £870 / £907 / £944. Every band keys to the mandatory five-plus threshold; no Part 3 or s.56 line. SEARCH TEST: the site search is server-side, honours quoted phrases and reports counts. '"selective licensing"' returned 'Results 1 - 5 of about 5' and '"additional licensing"' returned 'Results 1 - 3 of about 3'. All eight hits are the comparator table, civil-penalty boilerplate, a CON29O conveyancing form and LACORS fire guidance. SITEMAP TEST: 5,923 URLs pulled, ZERO contain 'selective'. TRAPS EXCLUDED, one severe: (1) ARTICLE 4. North Warwickshire confirmed a BOROUGH-WIDE HMO Article 4 Direction taking effect 2 March 2026. The sealed direction was read in full: made under article 4(1) of the GPDO 2015, First Schedule withdrawing permitted development for 'change of use of a building from a use falling within Class C3 (dwellinghouses) ... to a use falling within Class C4 (houses in multiple occupation)', Second Schedule 'Land being the area of North Warwickshire Borough as shown edged red', 'confirmed and shall take effect on 2 March 2026'. The document contains ZERO occurrences of the word 'licens'. Brand new, borough-wide and future-dated, so it reads exactly like a designation. It is planning control. Highest-risk false positive in this batch. (2) NEIGHBOUR BLEED, also severe: para 6.3 of the council's own report says 'Coventry City have in place an Article 4 Direction restricting HMO's in certain areas and have an Additional Licensing Scheme for small HMO's which took effect May 2025.' A domain-scoped keyword scrape of northwarks.gov.uk returns that sentence and could be misread as North Warwickshire having a scheme. It is Coventry's. The same table also shows Oadby and Wigston with selective 'Yes' and Warwick District with additional 'Yes', both hosted on North Warwickshire's site. (3) Civil-penalty boilerplate: the enforcement procedure lists 'Offences in relation to the Selective Licensing of houses [Section 95 Housing Act 2004]' and, explicitly conditional, 'Offences in relation to the licensing of HMOs or houses if Selective Licensing is in force'. SHARED SERVICE: Nuneaton and Bedworth accepts licence applications for both authorities. Both were verified separately and neither has a designation. LIMITATIONS: general web search was unavailable and external engines were bot-blocked, so no external index cross-check for an orphan page outside the sitemap. Committee agendas were not paged back to 2006.

E07000134.research: The council's Housing Enforcement Policy, under 'The Licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation', states 'Mandatory requirements for licensing apply only to houses (or flats) that are in multiple occupation' and then 'The Council has discretionary powers to introduce licensing for other residential accommodation through additional or selective licensing schemes.' The construction 'has discretionary powers to INTRODUCE' describes an unexercised power; no designated area, commencement date or fee appears anywhere. FEE TEST: the licence page states 'A property needs a mandatory HMO licence if it is both: A HMO [and] Occupied by five people or more who do not form a single household', then 'There is an initial fee of £410.00 payable with the submission of the application' and 'If an officer intends to grant a licencse, a further fee of £537.00 will be required before the licence is issued' (council's own typo). Two fee lines, both mandatory. COMMITTEE TEST: the ModernGov search works but ONLY via POST with the full hidden field set plus a Referer header; a GET silently returns the blank form, which would look like a false nil return. Driven correctly, '"selective licensing"' returned 6 documents (2019 Cabinet HMO policy, 2023 scrutiny and cabinet private sector housing policies, three Audit and Governance boilerplate items) and '"additional licensing"' returned ZERO. No designation report exists in the committee record. SITEMAP TEST: 923 URLs, ZERO contain 'selective'; the sitemap does include the HMO and landlord pages, so coverage is genuine rather than thin. PIPELINE CHECK: the landlord services consultations page states 'There are no policies currently under review', last updated 22 June 2026. TRAPS EXCLUDED: (1) Article 4 at Kegworth (confirmed 23 July 2020, in force 19 February 2021, whole village, C3 to C4). Planning, not licensing. (2) Neighbour bleed: Leicester City has selective licensing; nothing from Leicester City was attributed here. (3) Civil-penalty boilerplate: 'Section 95 - Offences in relation to licensing of houses under Part 3 (inc. selective licensing)'. (4) Generic legal-framework description: the 2019 Cabinet HMO Licensing Policy lists all three regimes as 'the different types of licenses introduced in the Housing Act 2004', a textbook summary; the recommendation adopted only mandatory fees, room sizes, civil penalties and banning orders. (5) NAMING TRAP: 'Landlord Services Consultations' means the council acting as social landlord to its own tenants, not private rented licensing. (6) Voluntary accreditation via EMLAS. LIMITATIONS: the council's own site search sits behind a JavaScript bot gate and returns no server-side results, so its nil return carried no weight. No reachable consolidated corporate fees schedule exists, so the published HMO service-page fees were used, which are the operative charges. General web search was unavailable.

E07000148.research: Norwich's HMO licensing FAQs state: 'Part 2 of the Housing Act 2004 requires Norwich City Council to license certain HMOs in the private rented sector. Licensing was introduced in April 2006 ... In October 2018, the definition of HMO requiring a licence was extended by the Secretary of State to include HMOs with five or more occupants.' Part 2 mandatory only, with no Part 3 anywhere. On the requirement: 'You will require a licence for an HMO when all of the following apply: ... it is occupied by five or more people (including children).' The overview page says 'If the property is home to five or more people, it must be licensed under the national mandatory scheme' and, DECISIVELY AGAINST s.56, 'Safety Standards: we enforce rules around fire safety, electrical checks, and proper amenities - even for HMOs that don't require a licence.' If additional licensing were designated, sub-five HMOs WOULD require a licence; Norwich states they do not. FEE TEST: 'The HMO licence application fee is £1,141, split into two parts: [£636] ... £505 payable once your application has been processed (this covers a 5-year licence)'. A single mandatory fee, no Part 3 or s.56 cost-recovery line. STRUCTURAL TEST: the Licensing section index lists only animal activity, other regulatory licences, pavement, premises and alcohol, taxi and private hire, plus HMOs; 'other regulatory licences' covers street trading, skin piercing, sex establishments, gambling and charitable collections only. /selective-licensing returns 404 and the sitemap contains no 'selective' URL. TRAPS EXCLUDED: (1) 'The Licensing and Management of Houses in Multiple Occupation (ADDITIONAL PROVISIONS) (England) Regulations 2007' is cited in the FAQs for converted flats. Despite the word 'Additional' this is a management-standards instrument, NOT s.56. (2) The 2025 news item 'Council consulting on updated multiple-occupation housing policy' is a consultation on the ADMINISTRATION of the existing mandatory scheme, not a new designation. It states plainly 'It is only large HMOs that need a licence', and the listed changes are simpler administration, more detail on required information, 'removal of the one- and three-year licence options, all licences will now be five-year licences', and a risk-based approach to breaches. A consultation on a licensing POLICY is not a designation. (3) The closed-consultation register includes an 'Article 4 direction offices residential' item, which is office-to-residential planning control, unrelated to HMOs. LIMITATIONS: Norwich's sitewide search is fuzzy and does not honour quoted phrases; 'selective licensing' returned 141 pages led by allotment policies and a tenants' magazine article about drones, so it is worthless as a nil test and carried no weight. cmis.norwich.gov.uk returned 403 and norwich.moderngov.co.uk returned 522, so committee papers could not be searched. The published sitemap holds only 335 URLs, which is small for the site, so it may not be exhaustive. I could not locate a current Norwich HMO Article 4 page on the rebuilt site and am not asserting Norwich's Article 4 position either way; it does not affect the licensing verdict.

E07000219.research: VERIFIED NEGATIVE, with an active but preliminary member-level discussion that has produced no designation. S12000023.research: RESOLVED BY STATUTE, NOT BY PER-COUNCIL RESEARCH, and that distinction matters. Selective licensing (Housing Act 2004 Part 3) and additional HMO licensing (Part 2 s.56) exist only where that Act applies. Section 270(11) provides that "this Act extends to England and Wales only" (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2004/34/section/270). Orkney Islands therefore has no legal power to designate either scheme, so this is a definite answer rather than an absence of evidence, and it cannot change without primary legislation at Westminster. Scottish councils have NO power to designate selective or additional licensing areas. The Housing Act 2004 extends to England and Wales only (s.270(11)). Landlord registration and HMO licensing apply nationally instead. WHAT DOES APPLY INSTEAD. (1) LANDLORD REGISTRATION under the Antisocial Behaviour etc. (Scotland) Act 2004 Part 8: all landlords must register with each council where they let (exemptions: resident landlords, holiday lets, agricultural tenancies); joint owners must all register; adverts must show the registration number. Registration lasts 3 years and costs about £85 per council plus £20 per property (no per-property fee where the property is a licensed HMO), with a £170 late fee and a maximum penalty of £50,000. (2) HMO LICENSING under the Housing (Scotland) Act 2006 Part 5 s.125: 3+ persons who are not all members of the same family or of one or other of two families (i.e. 3+ households), sharing a basic amenity, as only or main residence. Licences typically run 3 years, the fee is set by each council, and the maximum penalty is £50,000. NOTE THE THRESHOLD DIFFERENCE: Scotland's HMO test is THREE or more people from three or more households, which is broader than England's mandatory five. TRAP EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED: Enhanced Enforcement Areas (Housing (Scotland) Act 2014 ss.27-28) are area-designated but are NOT a licence; they grant extra discretionary enforcement powers only. Enhanced Enforcement Areas are the single most likely thing to be mistaken for selective licensing in Scotland, because they are area-designated and housing-related, but they confer no licence requirement on any landlord.

W06000009.research: NEGATIVE, SOURCED, WITH AN EXPRESS COUNCIL STATEMENT. The Housing Act 2004 says that certain types of larger HMOs must be licensed - this is Mandatory Licensing. This covers HMOs that are: Three or more storeys high and, Are occupied by 5 or more persons who do not form a single household.' This retains the Welsh three-storey test. E07000122.research: VERIFIED NEGATIVE for the current position, with a genuine expired history. This was the highest-prior council in the batch (mill-town terraced stock in Nelson, Brierfield and Colne) and was dug into rather than accepting a quick nil. FEE TEST: the 'Do I need a licence?' page describes mandatory licensing ONLY: pre-October 2018 'at least 3 storeys high' with 'at least 5 tenants' forming 'more than 1 household' sharing 'toilet, bathroom or kitchen facilities', extended from 1 October 2018 to 'all HMOs with 5 or more tenants, making up 2 or more households, and which share some facilities' regardless of storeys. Fees: 'Application fee of £590' and 'Licence fee of £296' (total £886), and 'The licence is valid for five years'. No selective or s.56 line. NAVIGATION TEST: the Landlords section lists 18 items covering energy efficiency, possession, deposits, ASB, rent arrears, safety topics and HMOs, with NO selective licensing entry. The A-Z under 'S' lists sandbags through street trading with no selective licensing entry. SEARCH TEST, done carefully because Pendle's search misbehaves: the quoted-phrase search is BROKEN, returning 0 results for '"selective licensing"' but ALSO 0 for the control phrase '"houses in multiple occupation"' which demonstrably exists on the site, so that nil return was discarded entirely. The unquoted search does OR matching (710 results dominated by Licensing Act 2003 and taxi content), equally useless. The discriminating test was the SINGLE WORD 'selective', which returned exactly 4 results: Information 0, Downloads 0, Services 0, News 0, Meeting Minutes 4. Zero live service pages anywhere on the site. SITEMAP TEST: 11,252 URLs, ZERO contain 'selective'. HISTORY: the four hits are all archived Executive attachments: 'Item 4 Selective Licensing' (22 January 2015), 'Item 14 Selective Licensing Update' (22 October 2015), 'Item 12 Proposed Selective Licensing for the Waterside Area (including Appendices)' (17 March 2016), and 'Item 11 Proposed Colne Selective Licensing Area' plus 'Item 11 Revised Appendix 3 - List of Streets' (16 March 2017). The most recent is March 2017. A Part 3 designation lasts a maximum of five years, so even a scheme commenced immediately after that report would have expired by 2022, and nothing appears in the committee record since. No expired scheme object was recorded because confirmed commencement and end dates could not be established from the committee index alone. TRAPS EXCLUDED: expired-schemes-presented-as-live is precisely the risk here and was avoided by dating the last committee activity; neighbour bleed guarded against, as Burnley borders Pendle and nothing from Burnley was used. LIMITATIONS: the archived committee attachment pages expose only document titles and file sizes, not extractable text, so the Waterside and Colne designation instruments could not be read to confirm exact commencement and expiry dates. The finding is that nothing is live today, which is what a landlord needs; precise historical dates are not asserted. NOTE FOR THE DATASET: Pendle's historic designations were street-based (the Colne report carried a 'List of Streets' appendix) rather than ward-based, so they would not have been ward-matchable in any event.
